description: Organize external references into sections and enrich links with fetched titles, descriptions and cached thumbnails.
description_html:
Link Collection

Organize multiple external references into a structured Moodle activity with sections, metadata and cached thumbnails.

Build curated collections

Teachers create ordered sections such as weekly material, references or further reading and add multiple external links to each section. This keeps related resources together instead of filling the course page with separate URL activities.

When a link is saved, the plugin can retrieve useful page metadata and present the student view as a compact list of enriched references.

Main features
  • Multiple ordered sections inside one activity.
  • Multiple ordered links inside each section.
  • Metadata extraction from page title, description, Open Graph and Twitter Card tags.
  • Cached thumbnails stored through Moodle's file system.
  • Manual title and description overrides.
  • One-click metadata refresh for teachers.
  • Moodle cURL security checks for page and image URLs.
  • Activity completion by view.
Cleaner course organization

Link Collection is useful for reading lists, research references, weekly resources, curated websites and any course area where a teacher wants to maintain a group of external materials as one coherent activity.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Link Collection organizes related web resources into a single course activity, reducing the need to create a long list of separate URL resources for one topic. Teachers can group references and maintain a coherent collection as readings or tools change. Learners benefit from having an annotated set of destinations rather than hunting through messages for the latest links. Administrators and teachers still need to check external-link availability, access restrictions and whether the destination is appropriate for the class.

name: Video Compare
description: Compare two or more videos side by side, answer comparison questions and create timestamp-to-timestamp comparisons.
description_html:
Video Compare

Put two or more videos into one activity so learners can compare content, answer questions and connect precise moments across sources.

Comparison as the learning task

Teachers add multiple videos and create required comparison questions. Questions can also be anchored to moments in two videos, helping learners compare specific evidence rather than relying only on a general impression.

Learners can watch videos side by side when screen space allows, switch between sources quickly and create timestamp-to-timestamp comparisons.

Independent tracking for every video
  • Uploaded videos, direct video URLs, YouTube and Vimeo.
  • Separate watched-segment tracking for each video.
  • Resume from the learner's latest position.
  • Overall activity progress calculated from the individual video progress values.
  • Required comparison questions.
  • Timestamp comparisons linking evidence from different videos.
Teacher reporting

Reports combine per-video viewing progress, overall progress, completion of required questions, learner answers and timestamp comparisons. This makes the activity useful for comparing demonstrations, cases, techniques, perspectives or before/after examples.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Video Compare is intended for learning tasks where two or more recordings must be considered together. Instead of expecting learners to remember a detail after switching tabs, the activity supports side-by-side comparison, questions and timestamp-based references. Teachers can ask participants to contrast technique, argument or outcome at particular moments. The comparison works best when the prompts specify what evidence students should seek and when the selected videos are available on the devices learners actually use.

name: Exit Ticket
description: Collect a short end-of-class formative reflection and review participation and responses in a teacher report.
description_html:
Exit Ticket

Collect a short private reflection at the end of a class and give teachers a fast overview of participation and understanding.

Two or three focused questions

Teachers configure a small set of open questions for the end of a lesson or class meeting. Each learner submits one private response containing their answers, keeping the activity deliberately lightweight.

When enabled, the learner can continue editing the response until the configured closing time.

A class-oriented report
  • Submission totals for the activity.
  • List of learners who have not yet responded.
  • Response rate for quick participation monitoring.
  • Answers grouped by question for easier review.
  • One activity instance can represent one specific class or lesson.
Useful for formative feedback

Exit Ticket supports quick end-of-class checks such as the most important idea learned, what remains unclear, or what should be revisited next. Because each instance represents one meeting, the course activity index can also serve as a simple history of class-by-class reflections.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Exit Ticket provides a lightweight way to collect a learner's immediate understanding or unresolved question at the end of a lesson. It is suitable for short formative responses that help teachers plan the next meeting rather than a full graded examination. In practice, a teacher can invite each participant to name one idea they understood and one point that remains unclear, then review the collected answers for recurring issues. The activity's value comes from closing the feedback loop, not simply accumulating one-line submissions.

name: Kopere Trail
description: Organize Moodle courses and other resources into larger learning trails without replacing Moodle's native completion and grading.
description_html:
Kopere Trail

Organize Moodle courses and external learning resources into larger learning journeys without replacing Moodle's native courses, activities, completion or grades.

A learning layer above individual courses

Kopere Trail gives learners a single journey that can span several Moodle courses and other resource types. The trail becomes the entry point, while the actual learning objects continue to live in their native systems.

Courses keep their own activities, completion rules, grades and competencies. The trail simply arranges those elements into stages and presents progress across the larger journey.

Extensible trail items

Trail stages can point to Moodle courses, URLs, HTML content, H5P and other item types provided through the plugin's subplugin architecture. This makes the trail model extensible without forcing every type of content into the core local plugin.

Enrollment and progress
  • Learners enter through the trail instead of navigating course by course.
  • Course-based items continue to use Moodle's own enrollment and access rules.
  • Progress can reflect the state of the underlying learning items.
  • The administrative interface lets managers build and order the larger learning journey.
  • Subplugins can add new kinds of trail items without replacing the main trail workflow.
Designed for programs and pathways

Kopere Trail is useful when one learning experience is larger than a single Moodle course: onboarding paths, certification journeys, corporate programs, curricula and other structured sequences can be represented without duplicating the courses themselves.

name: Video Annotation
description: Let learners attach notes, classifications and answers to exact moments or intervals in a video.
description_html:
Main features
Point and interval annotations

Learners can mark one exact moment or a start/end interval and return directly to that location by clicking the annotation.

Classification and prompts

Annotations can be classified and can answer teacher-defined prompts instead of functioning as unstructured notes only.

Aggregate timeline

Teachers can review annotations per learner and inspect an aggregate timeline to identify the parts of the video that attracted the most annotations.

Watched-segment tracking

The activity stores actual watched segments and a resume position, giving progress data that is more meaningful than the furthest position reached.

Completion rules

Completion can depend on watched percentage and on required annotation prompts.

Learning review

Annotations remain connected to their video context, making it practical to revisit evidence, comments and answers without manually searching the timeline.

Supported sources
Protected Moodle upload Direct video/HLS URL YouTube Vimeo
Moodle integration
  • Moodle backup and restore support.
  • Moodle Privacy API support.
  • Resume position storage.
  • Requires Moodle 4.4 or newer.
Why this activity exists

Video Annotation mantém cada comentário ligado à evidência audiovisual que o originou. O estudante pode marcar um ponto exato ou um intervalo, classificar a anotação, responder a prompts definidos pelo professor e voltar diretamente ao trecho correspondente ao clicar na anotação.

Learning flow
1. Teacher defines the focus

Prompts and annotation categories guide what learners should observe.

2. Learner watches

Video progress is tracked while the learner analyzes the material.

3. Evidence is annotated

A note can reference one exact moment or an interval.

4. Patterns are reviewed

Teachers can inspect individual annotations and aggregate concentration along the timeline.

What learners can do
Point annotation

Attach a response to one exact second.

Interval annotation

Represent evidence that develops over a period.

Prompts

Teacher-defined prompts turn annotation into a guided task.

Classification

Annotations can be organized by purpose or analytical category.

Timeline navigation

Selecting an annotation returns playback to its referenced evidence.

Aggregate timeline

Identify the video regions that generated the most annotations across the class.

Tracking and evidence

The activity tracks actual watched segments and stores a resume position, while every annotation keeps its temporal context. Point annotations preserve one timestamp and interval annotations preserve both start and end, which means the teacher does not need to manually search the video to understand what the learner was referring to.

Teacher reports
Per learner

Review all annotations created by one student.

Prompt status

See whether required annotation prompts were completed.

Aggregate concentration

Identify timeline regions with a high density of annotations.

Watched percentage

Relate annotation behavior to real viewing progress.

Contextual review

Return directly to the exact evidence referenced by an annotation.

Completion

Combine watched percentage with required annotation prompts.

Typical uses
Video critiqueTeacher educationClinical observationMedia literacyResearch codingEvidence-based discussion

name: Video Debate
description: Run evidence-based debates where students support arguments with precise excerpts from tracked video content.
description_html:
Video Debate

Run structured debates in which arguments and replies are grounded in precise evidence selected from a video.

Evidence-based discussion

The teacher defines the debate question and available positions. Learners choose or receive a position, publish an initial argument with one or more video evidence references and then reply to classmates.

Evidence is tied to the tracked video, allowing discussion to point back to exact moments rather than relying on vague references to the content.

Video, discussion and assessment together
  • Uploaded video, direct URL, YouTube and Vimeo sources.
  • Server-authoritative watched-segment tracking and resume.
  • Timeline markers for debate evidence.
  • Moodle groups and publish-before-viewing-peers workflow.
  • Weighted grading with teacher feedback and gradebook integration.
  • Completion rules, participation reports and moderation tools.
  • Moodle notifications, event logging, course reset, backup/restore and Privacy API support.
  • Transcript support and optional WebVTT captions for HTML5 video sources.
Protecting timestamp integrity

If the teacher changes the source video or its canonical duration after learner data exists, the plugin requires explicit confirmation and clears video-dependent progress, evidence and stored grades. This prevents old timestamps from silently referring to different content.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Video Debate puts an argument-and-response workflow around recorded contributions. Teachers can define a proposition or topic and ask participants to defend, challenge or respond to an idea using short video evidence. The key distinction from a playlist is that contributions belong to a structured exchange, and the relationship between a claim and its responses remains visible. Teachers should communicate participation expectations, deadlines and moderation rules so that the activity supports reasoned discussion rather than merely accumulating disconnected recordings.

name: Video Answer
description: Collect short webcam or phone-camera video responses recorded directly in the browser.
description_html:
Video Answer

Collect short learner video responses recorded directly from a computer or phone camera inside Moodle.

A simple spoken-video response workflow

Teachers create a prompt such as explaining a concept, demonstrating a short response or presenting an idea, then choose the recording limit. Learners record with the browser camera and microphone, preview the result and submit it without leaving the activity.

Main features
  • Recording limits of 30, 60 or 120 seconds.
  • Camera and microphone capture directly in the browser.
  • Preview before submission.
  • Optional re-recording or replacement of the current response.
  • One current submission per learner.
  • Protected storage through Moodle's File API.
  • Teacher report with learner, duration, submission time and video playback.
  • Privacy API integration.
Useful for concise audiovisual evidence

Video Answer is suitable for short oral explanations, language practice, reflections, quick demonstrations and other activities where a brief recorded response is more appropriate than a text submission.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Video Answer collects a short recorded response through the browser or device camera, lowering the friction of assignments that are easier to demonstrate orally or visually than in text. It can support language practice, presentations and explanation of a process, provided learners know the recording duration and submission requirements. Teachers can review the answer as part of the course activity instead of gathering files through external channels. Camera and microphone permissions, supported formats and device compatibility need testing for the intended participants.

name: Confidence Level
description: Collect a four-level confidence self-assessment and compare initial and later responses for metacognitive reflection.
description_html:
Confidence Level

Capture how confident learners feel about a topic and compare their initial and later self-assessment without turning the activity into a graded test.

Four confidence levels

Learners respond using four levels ranging from not knowing to feeling they have mastered the topic. Teachers can allow a second response after instruction, making it possible to compare the first and latest state as a simple metacognitive before/after signal.

The activity does not assign a grade and does not use AI. Its purpose is to make learner confidence visible as a teaching signal.

Live classroom reporting
  • Identified or anonymous responses.
  • Optional second response for before/after comparison.
  • Real-time report refreshed every few seconds.
  • Pie, bar and area chart views.
  • Teacher control over when learners may see aggregate results.
  • Opening and closing windows.
  • Optional same-public-IP presence validation.
  • Optional geolocation validation against a teacher reference point.
Anonymous mode without losing comparison

In anonymous mode the learner id is not stored with the response. The plugin uses an activity-specific pseudonymous HMAC value so it can compare a participant's first and latest answers without exposing identity in the report.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Confidence Level asks learners to express how confident they feel about a response or concept, producing a different signal from whether their answer is correct. Teachers can use this distinction to identify topics where students guess correctly, remain uncertain or are confident in an inaccurate conclusion. The activity fits short formative exercises and reflection. Confidence is self-reported and influenced by context, so it should complement rather than replace demonstrated knowledge, feedback and classroom conversation.

name: Before / After
description: Capture an initial idea and a later revised idea so conceptual change can be compared side by side.
description_html:
Before / After

Capture what a learner thought before an experience and what they think afterward, making conceptual change visible side by side.

Two moments of reflection

The learner first writes the initial response in the 'Before' stage. When the teacher decides the class is ready for the second reflection, the teacher releases the 'After' stage from the report.

At that moment the initial response is frozen so it remains an authentic record of the learner's earlier understanding rather than something that can be rewritten after seeing the new material.

Teacher view
  • Configurable prompts for the two reflection stages.
  • Manual release of the second stage.
  • Automatic freezing of the initial response when the second stage opens.
  • Side-by-side comparison for each learner.
  • Participation and completion counters.
  • Backup and restore of activity data.
  • Moodle Privacy API integration.
Designed for conceptual change

The activity is useful for lessons, debates, practical experiences and other situations where the teacher wants learners to make their change in thinking explicit without framing the exercise as a conventional test.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Before / After makes change visible by inviting a learner to respond before an instructional experience and return to the same topic afterward. This allows teachers to compare explanations, perceptions or answers over time instead of treating the final submission as the entire learning record. The usefulness depends on asking comparable questions and leaving room to explain what changed. A difference between two responses can support reflection, but it is not automatically a reliable measurement of long-term mastery.

name: Audio Answer
description: Collect short spoken answers recorded in the browser with configurable duration limits and teacher playback reports.
description_html:
Main features
Browser recording

Uses the MediaRecorder API and microphone access so learners can record without an external recording service.

Controlled duration

Teachers choose a 30, 60 or 120 second recording limit, and the browser automatically stops recording at the configured limit.

Preview and re-record

Learners can preview the recording before saving, and recording again replaces the current response.

Teacher playback report

Teachers get a report with one audio player for each learner response, making spoken answers quick to review.

Moodle file storage

Audio is stored through the Moodle File API rather than being sent to an external recording provider.

Automatic completion

The activity can optionally be marked complete automatically after the learner submits an audio answer.

Moodle integration
  • Capability checks and session-key validation.
  • MIME-type and upload-size validation.
  • Backup and restore support.
  • Moodle Privacy API support.
  • English and Brazilian Portuguese language packs.
  • Requires a modern browser with MediaRecorder/getUserMedia; microphone access normally requires HTTPS except on localhost.
Why this activity exists

Audio Answer cria uma atividade propositalmente simples para respostas faladas. O professor faz uma pergunta, define um limite de gravação e o estudante grava diretamente no navegador, escuta antes de salvar e mantém uma resposta atual que pode ser substituída por uma nova gravação.

Learning flow
1. Teacher asks one question

The activity remains focused on one spoken-response prompt.

2. Learner records in the browser

Microphone capture uses the browser MediaRecorder API.

3. Learner previews the answer

The recording can be listened to before it is saved.

4. Teacher reviews the report

Each learner appears with an embedded audio player.

What learners can do
30-second response

Use a compact recording window for rapid oral checks.

60-second response

Allow a moderate explanation while keeping review manageable.

120-second response

Support longer oral reasoning without becoming a full media assignment.

Preview

Learners can listen before saving.

Re-record

A new recording replaces the current response.

Moodle storage

Audio is stored through the Moodle File API instead of an external recorder.

Tracking and evidence

The browser stops recording at the configured duration. On submission, the server validates upload size, MIME type and the declared duration before accepting the response. The activity keeps one current recording per learner, which makes the report straightforward and avoids unnecessary attempt complexity.

Teacher reports
One player per learner

Listen to responses directly from the teacher report.

Current answer

The report always represents the learner latest saved recording.

Submission status

Identify learners who have already responded.

Automatic completion

Optionally complete the activity when an audio answer exists.

Moodle-managed files

Responses remain associated with the learner and activity.

Simple oral assessment

Use spoken evidence without adding a complex grading workflow.

Typical uses
Language learningPronunciation practiceOral reflectionOne-minute explanationsFormative checksSpoken accessibility alternatives

name: Video Book
description: Build a chapter-based multimedia book in which video is the primary learning medium and progress is tracked per chapter.
description_html:
Main features
Chapter-based structure

Create ordered chapters with a title, video, explanatory text, image, files or documents, captions and complementary links.

Chapter navigation

Students navigate through a chapter sidebar and Previous/Next controls, with either free navigation or a sequential flow.

Real progress per chapter

Each chapter can require a minimum watched percentage based on unique watched segments rather than the furthest playback position.

Clear chapter states

Chapters are represented as Not started, In progress or Completed, while the activity calculates overall progress from completed chapters.

Captions and materials

Supports WebVTT captions, automatic SRT-to-WebVTT conversion, images, rich text, PDFs/files and complementary links.

Reports and completion

Teachers get a student-by-chapter progress report, and Moodle activity completion can require all chapters to be completed.

Supported sources
Moodle upload Direct video/HLS URL YouTube Vimeo
Moodle integration
  • Resume from the last playback position automatically or after asking the learner.
  • Optional restriction prevents seeking into video sections not yet watched.
  • Backup and restore can include learner progress.
  • Moodle Privacy API support.
  • Requires Moodle 4.5 or newer.
Why this activity exists

Video Book organiza conteúdo audiovisual em capítulos e trata cada capítulo como uma unidade de aprendizagem completa. Vídeo, texto, imagem, arquivos, legendas e links permanecem juntos, enquanto o progresso é calculado individualmente por capítulo e consolidado no livro inteiro.

Learning flow
1. Chapters organize the course

The teacher creates an ordered multimedia structure instead of a loose sequence of unrelated activities.

2. Learners navigate the book

A chapter sidebar plus Previous and Next controls keeps the learning path visible.

3. Each chapter tracks progress

Not started, In progress and Completed states are calculated independently.

4. Overall progress is consolidated

The activity combines completed chapters into one Video Book progress view.

What learners can do
Multimedia chapter

Combine video, rich text, image, files, captions and complementary links.

Free navigation

Allow learners to move through chapters according to their needs.

Sequential navigation

Keep later chapters behind the intended pedagogical sequence.

Chapter threshold

Require a minimum percentage of unique watched video for each chapter.

Caption support

Use WebVTT captions and convert SRT captions to WebVTT when saved.

Supporting resources

Keep PDFs, documents and external links attached to the chapter they support.

Tracking and evidence

The browser sends short contiguous playback intervals and the server merges them into unique watched content for the current chapter. Seeking alone does not increase progress. The latest position can be restored and, when seeking restriction is enabled, previously watched portions remain available while unseen portions can stay protected.

Teacher reports
Student by chapter

See progress for every learner across the complete book structure.

Chapter state

Identify chapters that are not started, in progress or completed.

Watched percentage

Inspect unique watched-video percentage for each chapter.

Overall progress

See how completed chapters contribute to the whole activity.

Completion

Require all chapters before Moodle considers the activity complete.

Persistent progress

Learner chapter progress can be included in backup and restore data.

Typical uses
Video-first coursesMicrolearning collectionsTechnical manualsLong-form trainingRecorded classesStructured audiovisual libraries

name: Video Checkpoints
description: Insert mandatory or optional checkpoints into video playback using confirmations, answers, keywords or choices.
description_html:
Main features
Flexible checkpoints

Place checkpoints by exact time or video percentage and make each one mandatory or optional.

Five response styles

A checkpoint can request a confirmation, simple answer, keyword, short answer or a choice between configured options.

Real viewing tracking

Stores unique watched segments, total playback time, watched percentage, last position and the learner's most recent access.

Seeking rules

Seeking can remain unrestricted or be limited to portions of the video the learner has already watched.

Completion rules

Completion can require every checkpoint or a configurable minimum number of completed checkpoints.

Teacher report

The report shows watched percentage, completed and pending checkpoints, last access and current activity status for each learner.

Supported sources
Moodle File API upload Direct browser-playable video URL YouTube Vimeo
Moodle integration
  • Resume position is stored for the learner.
  • YouTube uses the IFrame Player API.
  • Vimeo uses the Player API.
  • Requires Moodle 4.4 or later.
Why this activity exists

Video Checkpoints insere interações obrigatórias ou opcionais diretamente no fluxo do vídeo. O checkpoint pode aparecer em um tempo exato ou percentual do vídeo e pedir confirmação, resposta simples, palavra-chave, resposta curta ou escolha, sem obrigar o professor a criar um quiz separado para pequenas verificações.

Learning flow
1. Checkpoints are positioned

The teacher defines where each checkpoint appears and whether it is mandatory.

2. Learner watches normally

The activity records contiguous watched segments and the latest playback position.

3. Interaction appears in context

The learner responds without leaving the video activity.

4. Progress is consolidated

The report combines viewing progress, completed checkpoints, pending checkpoints and last access.

What learners can do
Exact-time checkpoint

Place an interaction at a specific second of the video.

Percentage checkpoint

Anchor a checkpoint proportionally to total video duration.

Confirmation

Ask the learner to explicitly acknowledge a statement or task.

Simple answer

Collect one direct response without creating another activity.

Keyword

Require a focused keyword when recognition is enough.

Choice

Present configured alternatives for a quick decision.

Tracking and evidence

Video Checkpoints stores unique watched segments rather than treating movement of the playhead as viewing. It also records total playback time, watched percentage and last position. Repeated viewing remains visible through total time, while only newly watched content increases the unique percentage.

Teacher reports
Watched percentage

See how much unique video content each learner consumed.

Completed checkpoints

Identify interactions already completed.

Pending checkpoints

See which checkpoints still require a response.

Last access

Track the latest learner activity in the video.

Activity status

Combine checkpoint progress into one learner status.

Completion

Require every checkpoint or a configurable minimum number.

Typical uses
Compliance videosLong lecturesProcedural demonstrationsOrientation contentSafety trainingQuick comprehension checks

name: Video Practice
description: Provide a reference demonstration video and let learners submit or record their own practice video.
description_html:
Video Practice

Combine a reference demonstration with learner video practice, structured stages and rubric-style teacher assessment.

Watch, practice and submit

The teacher provides a reference video that demonstrates a procedure, technique or practical task. Learners watch the reference and then upload or record their own video performing the same practice.

Reference viewing is tracked by watched intervals, so progress reflects portions actually played instead of simply the furthest playback position reached.

Structured practical assessment
  • Reference video from Moodle upload, direct URL, YouTube or Vimeo.
  • Tracked reference viewing and resume.
  • Teacher-defined stages such as preparation, organization, execution and finalization.
  • Instructions and maximum score for each stage.
  • Video upload or in-browser camera/microphone recording.
  • Draft replacement before submission.
  • Fixed or unlimited attempt policies.
  • Teacher ability to return an attempt for editing.
  • Final grade calculated from stage scores and sent to the Moodle gradebook.
For demonstration-based learning

Video Practice fits practical skills where learners need to observe a model, reproduce the technique and receive structured evaluation against the stages that matter.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Video Practice supports repeated learning from a video through a practical task rather than passive viewing alone. Teachers can connect a demonstration to an action or response, giving learners a structured opportunity to apply what they observed. When a task depends on a particular scene, clear instructions about the relevant point make the experience more useful. Completion should reflect the activity's configured task requirements, not an assumption that playback alone proves the skill has been acquired.

name: Quick Statistics
description: Calculate descriptive statistics instantly in the browser without storing the learner's entered values.
description_html:
Quick Statistics

Calculate descriptive statistics instantly inside Moodle while keeping learner-entered values entirely in the browser.

Descriptive statistics without leaving the course

Learners paste or type a sequence of numbers and immediately receive the main descriptive measures. The entered values are processed locally in the browser and are not stored in Moodle.

Available results
  • Count and sum.
  • Mean and median.
  • Mode, including multimodal datasets.
  • Minimum, maximum and range.
  • Population or sample variance.
  • Population or sample standard deviation.
  • Sorted values.
Flexible numeric input

Values can be separated by spaces, line breaks, tabs or semicolons, and comma-separated lists are also supported. Decimal values may use a point or comma, with the interface handling the ambiguity between a decimal comma and a list separator.

The activity is useful as a quick classroom calculator and as a companion to exercises where students need to inspect the underlying dataset and verify each descriptive measure.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Quick Statistics lets learners calculate descriptive measures using values they provide directly in the browser, which is useful while working through examples or checking hand calculations. Teachers can ask students to interpret the meaning of an average, spread or distribution and then compare their reasoning with the computed summary. Because user-entered values are not persisted as individual learner records, the activity functions as a calculation aid rather than a submission system. Privacy and interpretability both benefit from making that distinction clear.

name: Rule of Three
description: Explore simple and compound rule-of-three calculations interactively with step-by-step equations.
description_html:
Rule of Three

Explore simple and compound proportional calculations interactively and show the equation, substitution, factors and final result step by step.

Simple and compound proportion

Teachers choose the calculation mode, relationship type, initial values and decimal precision. Learners can then change values and see the related quantities recalculate immediately.

Simple mode supports direct or inverse proportion with four synchronized values. Compound mode adds two influencing quantities, each of which can use a direct or inverse relationship.

Learning-focused calculator
  • Direct and inverse simple rule of three.
  • Compound rule of three with two influencing quantities.
  • Synchronized values that recalculate while the learner experiments.
  • Step-by-step equation and substitution display.
  • Visible direct/inverse factors used in the calculation.
  • Configurable decimal precision.
  • Standard Moodle completion by activity view.
  • No learner calculation history is stored.
Useful beyond the final answer

Because the calculation process remains visible, the activity can be used to demonstrate proportional reasoning rather than acting only as a black-box calculator.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Rule of Three makes proportional reasoning inspectable through simple and compound examples, displaying the equation and intermediate arithmetic steps. Teachers can use it to demonstrate direct and inverse relationships instead of asking students to memorize an unexplained cross-multiplication pattern. A learner can change an input and observe how the calculated result follows from the chosen relation. It remains important to verify whether a real problem is actually proportional before applying the arithmetic mechanically.

name: Mass Mail Enrol
description: Enrol existing Moodle users into a course from a pasted list of email addresses with role and result controls.
description_html:
Mass Mail Enrol

Enroll existing Moodle users into a course by pasting a list of email addresses and receive a clear result for every entry.

Bulk enrollment from a simple list

Teachers or managers paste email addresses copied from another system, spreadsheet or message. The plugin accepts common separators, removes duplicates and resolves the addresses against existing Moodle accounts before enrollment.

Enrollment uses Moodle's manual enrollment API, and the current operator can select only roles they are actually allowed to assign.

Clear processing results
  • Comma, semicolon, whitespace and line-break separators.
  • Automatic duplicate removal.
  • Enrollment through Moodle's manual enrollment API.
  • Role choices limited by the operator's assignable roles.
  • Separate results for newly enrolled, already enrolled, not found, invalid, suspended and failed entries.
  • Course-navigation access controlled by the plugin capability.
  • No plugin-specific personal-data store.
Useful for operational enrollment

Mass Mail Enrol is suited to situations where an institution already has the users in Moodle but receives enrollment lists as email addresses and needs a faster alternative to processing those users one by one.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Mass Mail Enrol helps administrators coordinate communication and enrolment operations across groups of users without handling every recipient separately. Bulk actions have greater reach than individual course edits, so the important operational questions are who is eligible, what message will be sent and how errors are reported. Teams should preview recipient selection and ensure that repeated processing does not create unwanted duplication. Course permissions and organizational communication policies still apply when the interface makes an action faster.

name: Rank
description: Ask learners to rank a set of items and calculate the class average position of each item.
description_html:
Rank

Ask learners to order a small set of items and turn the class submissions into an average ranking for each option.

Ranking as the activity

Teachers define between five and ten items and a criterion such as priority, chronology, importance or process sequence. Learners reorder the items into their preferred or expected order and submit one ranking.

The interaction uses drag and drop with keyboard-friendly movement controls so the ordering task is not limited to pointer input.

Class-level result

The teacher report calculates the average position of every item across the class. This makes it possible to see both individual ordering choices and the collective tendency without manually combining each learner's ranking.

Useful for prioritization and sequencing

Rank can support prioritization exercises, ordered processes, chronology activities, consensus preparation and other tasks where the learning objective is expressed by the relative position of several alternatives.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Rank asks learners to order several options rather than select one preferred answer. Teachers can use it to surface relative priorities, negotiate criteria or discuss why participants disagree about an ordering. A collective average rank makes patterns visible but does not show every individual rationale, so it works well as the beginning of a discussion. Clear instructions about ties and the direction of the ranking help learners interpret their result and avoid treating an average position as an objective score.

name: Video Evidence
description: Answer questions using one or more evidence moments or intervals selected directly from a tracked video.
description_html:
Video Evidence

Require learners to answer questions with evidence selected from exact moments or intervals in a tracked video.

Evidence must point back to the video

Questions can ask for a single moment or a complete time interval. Learners select one or more pieces of evidence directly from the video and add a written justification for each selection.

Teachers can configure an expected time range with tolerance, allowing the system to score whether the selected excerpt falls in the intended part of the video while still leaving the quality of the explanation available for teacher assessment.

Video tracking and assessment
  • Moodle upload, direct URL/HLS, YouTube and Vimeo sources.
  • Real watched-segment tracking and playback resume.
  • Single-moment or interval evidence questions.
  • One or multiple evidence selections per question.
  • Written justification attached to every evidence item.
  • Optional expected ranges with tolerance for automatic selection scoring.
  • Independent weights for excerpt accuracy, justification quality and minimum evidence quantity.
  • Manual or hybrid grading with feedback and gradebook integration.
  • Completion rules for required evidence questions.
  • Per-learner report including answers, evidence, submissions, grade and watched percentage.
For evidence-based observation

Video Evidence is useful when learners should not only state an answer but demonstrate exactly where the supporting evidence appears in the audiovisual material.

How it fits real Moodle workflows

Video Evidence encourages learners to justify answers with identifiable moments or intervals from a source video. It is useful for analytical assignments where the strength of a claim depends on being able to point to what was actually shown. Instead of accepting a broad statement without support, a teacher can review the selected segment alongside the explanation. This does not guarantee that the interpretation is correct, but it makes the supporting observation inspectable and easier to discuss.

name: Video Sequence
description: Teach ordered processes by asking learners to reconstruct or reorder steps after watching a tracked video.
description_html:
Video Sequence

Teach ordered processes and procedures by asking learners to reconstruct the correct sequence after watching a tracked video.

Two sequence-learning modes

Teachers define the reference steps in their correct order and can attach descriptions, accepted alternative names and video start/end times to each step.

In reorder mode, learners receive the teacher-defined steps shuffled and put them back in order. In create mode, the reference names are hidden and learners reconstruct the sequence from memory.

Video-aware interaction
  • Uploaded video, direct URL, YouTube and Vimeo sources.
  • Server-side watched-progress tracking and resume.
  • Optional anti-skip behavior.
  • Minimum watched percentage before answering.
  • Step-linked timestamps.
  • Drag-and-drop ordering with keyboard-friendly move controls.
  • Accepted aliases for learner-created sequences.
  • Attempt limits and configurable feedback timing.
  • Automatic grading and Moodle completion rules.
Useful for procedures and ordered events

Video Sequence is suited to workflows, safety procedures, demonstrations, chronological events and other learning objectives where understanding the correct order is central to the task.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Sequence is useful when learners need to understand why a process follows a particular order. After studying a demonstration, students reconstruct or reorder its steps and can compare the resulting sequence with the expected procedure. Teachers should choose steps that have a meaningful dependency rather than unrelated labels that could be arranged arbitrarily. The activity can support process training, scientific methods and practical workflows. Reviewing the reasoning behind an incorrect order is often more valuable than simply telling the learner which sequence was right.

name: QR Code Check
description: Register attendance or participation from short-lived QR codes with session, timing and IP checks.
description_html:
QR Code Check

Record classroom participation with short-lived QR codes designed to reduce reuse and preserve attendance even when the learner still needs to sign in.

Short-lived attendance sessions

A teacher starts a projection session and displays a QR code that changes every ten seconds. Each generated code is accepted for a very short period, reducing the usefulness of screenshots or codes shared after the fact.

A valid scan is registered before authentication. If the learner still needs to log in, a one-time continuation keeps the original scan alive for a limited period so the attendance action is not lost during sign-in.

Session and attendance controls
  • Independent projection sessions for the same activity.
  • QR code rotation every 10 seconds with a maximum acceptance window of 20 seconds.
  • One-time continuation for authenticated completion after an anonymous scan.
  • Reference IP captured when the teacher starts the projection.
  • Report highlighting scans whose observed IP differs from the session reference.
  • Only the first confirmed attendance record per learner and session is retained.
  • Automatic cleanup of old pending scans.
Completion and audit trail

The activity can use successful attendance as a custom completion condition. Reports and restored course data preserve the historical attendance record, while restored sessions are closed and given new secrets so an old projected QR code cannot become valid again.

name: Pair
description: Form student pairs manually, randomly or through learner choice while preserving existing pairs and constraints.
description_html:
Pair

Form learner pairs inside a course through student choice, teacher randomization or a combination of both.

Three pairing modes

The activity can let learners choose an available classmate, let the teacher generate pairs randomly, or combine both approaches so students form some pairs themselves and the teacher allocates whoever remains.

Existing pairs are preserved when random pairing is run. If an odd number of learners remains available, one participant simply stays unpaired instead of forcing an invalid group.

Teacher controls
  • Student-choice, random or combined pairing modes.
  • Opening and closing dates.
  • Optional permission for learners to leave an existing pair.
  • Teacher report showing current pairs and unpaired learners.
  • Removal of a pair immediately makes both learners available again.
Simple partner allocation

Pair is useful for peer exercises, practice partners, review activities and other two-person work where teachers want a focused pairing workflow without manually creating Moodle groups for every pair.

Practical use and interpretation

Pair helps teachers organize two-person activities without relying on an informal list that quickly becomes outdated when enrolments change. Depending on the chosen method, pairs can be assigned by the teacher, generated or formed through learner choice, with existing assignments and constraints respected. The activity can support peer practice, language exchanges and joint projects. Teachers should explain whether pairs are fixed, whether changes are allowed and how unmatched learners will be handled so the pairing itself does not become the obstacle to participation.

name: Simple Journal
description: Provide one private editable reflection entry per learner with a simple teacher reading interface.
description_html:
Simple Journal

Give each learner one private reflection entry per activity using Moodle's standard editor and a deliberately lightweight workflow.

One private entry per learner

Each activity instance represents one journal or reflection prompt. Learners write a single private entry and may return to update it later.

The activity is intentionally simpler than an assignment: there is no grading workflow, no file submission and no peer visibility.

Teacher review
  • Moodle text editor for learner reflections.
  • One entry per learner and journal activity.
  • Private content that other learners cannot see.
  • Teacher capability for reviewing learner entries.
  • Simple learner selector for navigating reflections.
  • Backup and restore with user data.
  • Moodle Privacy API support.
For ongoing reflection

Simple Journal fits learning diaries, class reflections, personal observations and other activities where learners need a private writing space without the overhead of a full assignment.

Practical use and interpretation

Simple Journal gives each learner a private place to maintain a reflection entry inside the course, without the overhead of creating a forum topic or formal assignment for every thought. Teachers can use it for weekly reflection, reading notes or personal progress observations and review the content through the intended teacher interface. The important design distinction is between a learner's ongoing editable entry and a public discussion: privacy, feedback expectations and any completion requirements should be clear from the outset.

name: Video Discussion
description: Attach threaded discussions and teacher prompts to precise timestamps in a video.
description_html:
Video Discussion

Attach threaded discussion directly to exact moments in a video so comments, replies and teacher prompts stay connected to the evidence being discussed.

Discussion on the timeline

Learners can start a discussion at the current playback position, reply to classmates and jump from any discussion back to its timestamp. Timeline markers make the relationship between conversation and video visible during playback.

Teachers can also create predefined prompts at specific moments and mark selected prompts as mandatory.

Participation controls
  • Uploaded HTML5 video, direct URL, YouTube and Vimeo.
  • Resume playback and watched-segment tracking.
  • Learner-created timestamped discussions.
  • Teacher-created timestamped prompts.
  • Mandatory prompts.
  • Post-before-viewing-peers mode.
  • Separate and visible Moodle groups.
  • Highlighted responses.
  • Participation grading with Moodle gradebook integration.
Teacher reporting

Reports combine comments, replies, completion of mandatory prompts, watched percentage and grade, giving teachers one view of both video engagement and discussion participation.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Discussion makes a particular timestamp the starting point for a conversation. Instead of asking learners to remember an example after watching the entire recording, teachers can attach questions or discussion threads to the scene where the issue occurs. This works well for case studies, demonstrations and analysis of recorded practice. In the classroom, the teacher should frame each prompt around evidence visible at that moment, while keeping participation and moderation rules clear. A timestamped comment gives useful context but does not guarantee a sound interpretation.

name: Activity Signup
description: Allocate students to internal activity groups with capacities, waiting lists and teacher management.
description_html:
Activity Signup

Allocate learners to internal activity groups with capacity limits, waiting lists and controlled self-service changes.

Choose a group while places are available

When the activity is created, the teacher can generate a chosen number of signup groups with an initial capacity. Learners select an available group, and full groups can expose a waiting list when that option is enabled.

If a confirmed participant leaves, the first learner in that group's waiting list is promoted automatically.

Group management
  • Configurable number of internal signup groups.
  • Capacity limit for each group.
  • Optional waiting lists.
  • Automatic promotion when a place becomes available.
  • Teacher control over whether learners may change or cancel their signup.
  • Custom group names and individual capacities.
  • Optional group leader.
  • Group-setting control transferred to the designated leader when one exists.
Useful for sessions and team allocation

Activity Signup can support workshop slots, project teams, presentation groups and other course activities where places are limited and learners need a clear self-enrollment workflow.

Practical use and interpretation

Activity Signup provides a structured way to register interest or reserve participation in a course event or activity. Teachers can use it when a class needs to divide into limited sessions, practical groups or scheduled opportunities without manually collecting names across messages. Participants benefit from a clear enrollment or signup state and any configured capacity rules. The experience should explain deadlines, eligibility and what happens when spaces become unavailable, because those constraints matter more than simply displaying a registration button.

name: Request Help
description: Organize student help requests in a live queue with topics, statuses, response times and classroom resolution.
description_html:
Request Help

Create a classroom help queue so learners can request assistance without interrupting the session and teachers can work through requests in a clear order.

A queue for learner questions

Learners choose one of the configured subjects, describe the problem and submit a request. The teacher sees a central queue ordered by status and creation time instead of relying on raised hands, private messages or memory.

A teacher can claim a request, write a response, mark it as answered in class, resolve it or reopen it when more information is needed.

Main features
  • Configurable help subjects.
  • Open, Answered and Resolved statuses.
  • Automatic queue refresh.
  • Written conversation history.
  • Answered-in-class action when no typed reply is needed.
  • Teacher assignment and request claiming.
  • First-response time tracking.
  • Status and subject filters.
  • Learner view restricted to their own requests.
  • Optional learner resolve and reopen actions.
Useful during live teaching

Request Help is designed for classrooms, labs and practical sessions where several learners may need assistance at once. The queue makes waiting visible, preserves the history of support and helps teachers avoid overlooking quieter students.

Practical use and interpretation

Request Help lets a learner communicate that assistance is needed in the context of a Moodle course instead of relying entirely on informal messages. A well-defined help request can make the issue visible to an appropriate teacher or support role and provide a manageable starting point for follow-up. Teachers should explain the intended use, expected response time and whether a request should include a particular activity or problem. This is especially useful when several participants need assistance during the same session and staff must prioritize responses.

name: Forum Reactions
description: Add configurable AJAX reactions to standard Moodle forum posts while preserving forum visibility rules, privacy handling and batched reaction counts.
description_html:
Forum interactionNo mod_forum modification

Forum Reactions

Add lightweight reactions to Moodle's standard Forum activity without forking or patching mod_forum.

Reaction controls update through AJAX and are also attached to forum posts that appear dynamically after the page initially loads.

Administrator controls
  • Choose which reactions are available.
  • Allow one or multiple reactions per user/post.
  • Decide whether users may react to their own posts.
  • Keep counts aligned with Moodle forum visibility rules.
Lifecycle-aware: stored reactions are cleaned up when their forum post/activity is deleted and user data is exposed through Moodle's Privacy API.
Features in practice

Forum Reactions adds configurable emoji responses to ordinary Moodle Forum posts without modifying the core Forum module. Participants react with an AJAX control, and counts are loaded in batches for visible posts, including posts inserted dynamically while discussions expand. Administrators choose the available reactions and whether participants may react more than once or to their own posts. Teachers can use these quick responses as informal signals, while longer conversations remain in Moodle's regular threads. Forum permissions and visibility rules still apply: a reaction should not expose a hidden post. Reactions are not an assessment of whether a message is correct or whether its author understood a topic.

Practical use and interpretation

Because this enhancement operates inside standard Forum, the practical rollout is to enable only reactions that suit the institution's tone and to check permissions for each type of forum visibility. Quick emoji feedback can lower the barrier to participation, but it should not be used as a substitute for explaining an argument in threaded conversation. The reaction data describes participant selections rather than an objective score assigned to a post.

name: Triangle Calculator
description: Solve triangle measurements interactively and display derived values, constraints and calculation steps.
description_html:
Triangle Calculator

Solve triangles from known sides and angles, redraw the geometry and show the calculations used to obtain the missing measurements.

Work from the measurements you know

Learners enter the available sides and angles. The calculator determines which geometric case applies, solves the remaining measurements directly in the browser and redraws the triangle as the values change.

Input constraints update dynamically so the interface can guide the learner according to the current triangle configuration.

Supported cases
  • SSS — three known sides.
  • SAS — two sides and the included angle.
  • ASA and AAS — two angles and a side.
  • SSA — including detection of the ambiguous case.
More than a numeric solver

The activity also presents derived geometric values and calculation steps, making it useful for exploring why a triangle solution works instead of returning only the final side and angle values.

Practical use and interpretation

Triangle Calculator helps learners connect known measurements with derived geometric values and the constraints needed for a valid triangle. Teachers can use it alongside geometry examples where students need to calculate unknown sides or angles, check consistency and inspect intermediate steps. A calculated value is useful only when the supplied measurements form a valid configuration, so the activity's constraints should be part of the lesson rather than hidden behind the answer. It supports guided calculation, not a replacement for proving a geometric relationship.

name: Video Summary
description: Combine tracked video viewing with structured summaries, timestamp references, grading and completion rules. Requires Video Bridge.
description_html:
Also requires Video Bridge.

Video Summary

Turn tracked video viewing into a structured synthesis task with drafts, final submissions and references back to exact moments in the video.

Summaries connected to evidence

Learners watch a tracked video, resume from their previous position and write a summary using the structure selected by the teacher. Parts of the summary can reference precise timestamps or intervals, and those references can be clicked to return to the source moment.

The activity supports draft and final submission states so learners can refine their synthesis before submitting.

Configurable summary formats
  • Free summary.
  • Maximum-word summary.
  • Five key points.
  • Three concepts.
  • Conclusion format.
  • Chapter-based summary.
  • Minimum number of video references.
  • Word and character limits.
Tracking, grading and completion

Teachers can grade with simple criteria and send the result to the Moodle gradebook. Completion can depend on watched percentage, final submission or both, while reports show viewing progress, draft/submission state, references, grade and status.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Summary asks learners to turn viewing into a coherent written synthesis tied to the actual content. Teachers can choose a summary format, limits and whether selected claims should reference exact moments. Learners may draft and revise before final submission, while grading and completion can reflect both the written work and watched coverage. Timestamp references are especially useful during feedback because teachers can inspect the source moment rather than guessing which passage the learner described. Summarizing the material is a different skill from merely reaching the end of playback.

name: Video Mission
description: Turn a video into a mission-based activity with required or optional tasks tied to moments, intervals and questions.
description_html:
Main features
Six mission types

Create missions for a video moment, a video interval, a question, an observation, repeated occurrences or a simple task confirmation.

Mission rules and points

Mark missions as mandatory or optional, assign points and choose whether learners may complete them in any order or sequentially.

Real viewing progress

Tracks unique watched segments, total playback time, watched percentage and the learner's last position instead of assuming that reaching the end means the whole video was watched.

Reports and grading

Teachers can review mission status, responses, selected moments, earned points and watched percentage for each learner, with grades synchronized to the Moodle gradebook.

Completion rules

Activity completion can require all mandatory missions, a minimum watched percentage, or both.

Resume and seeking control

Playback can resume from the stored position and the activity can restrict seeking into portions of the video the learner has not yet watched.

Supported sources
Moodle upload Direct HTTP/HTTPS video URL YouTube Vimeo
Moodle integration
  • Backup and restore support.
  • Moodle Privacy API support.
  • External AJAX functions.
  • English and Brazilian Portuguese language packs.
  • Mustache templates and AMD JavaScript.
Why this activity exists

Video Mission transforma o vídeo em uma atividade orientada por objetivos. Em vez de considerar o play como participação suficiente, o professor define missões que exigem que o estudante encontre evidências, selecione momentos, delimite intervalos, responda perguntas, registre observações ou confirme tarefas.

Learning flow
1. Video as the context

The video is the source material and the timeline becomes part of the activity, not merely a media player.

2. Missions define the objective

Each mission tells the learner what must be found, explained, confirmed or observed.

3. Evidence is stored

Responses can include text, exact moments, intervals and repeated occurrence timestamps.

4. Progress is consolidated

The activity combines mission status, points and real watched-video progress.

What learners can do
Moment mission

The learner identifies one exact point in the video where the requested event or evidence occurs.

Interval mission

The learner defines a start and end point when the relevant evidence spans a period.

Question mission

A textual answer can be attached to the learning objective without separating it from the video activity.

Observation mission

The learner records an interpretation or observation based on the audiovisual evidence.

Occurrence mission

The activity can require several occurrences of the same event and preserve every selected timestamp.

Confirmation mission

A lightweight confirmation can be used when the mission represents a concrete task or verification.

Tracking and evidence

The tracking model stores unique watched segments, total playback time, last position and watched percentage. Rewatching does not artificially increase the unique percentage, while the total playback time still records repeated study. Seeking can also be restricted so the learner cannot jump far beyond portions already watched.

Teacher reports
Mission status

See completed, pending and locked missions for each learner.

Answers and evidence

Review text responses, moments, intervals and repeated occurrences.

Points

See points earned per mission and the consolidated score.

Viewing progress

Compare mission completion with the percentage of unique video content actually watched.

Gradebook

Mission points can be synchronized with the Moodle gradebook.

Completion

Completion can require mandatory missions, a minimum watched percentage, or both.

Typical uses
Case-based learningTechnical demonstrationsClinical observationMedia analysisProcedural trainingEvidence-finding activities

name: Video Interview
description: Run sequential or conditional video interviews with text, uploaded media or browser-recorded responses.
description_html:
Video Interview

Build sequential or conditional interview activities with recorded prompts and text, audio or video learner responses.

Question-by-question interview flow

Teachers create an interview sequence using fixed or conditional progression. Questions can use recorded video prompts, while learners respond with text, uploaded audio or video, or in-browser recording when the browser supports MediaRecorder.

Per-question time limits help keep responses focused and make the activity suitable for interview practice, oral assessment and scenario-based questioning.

Attempts and assessment
  • Fixed or conditional question sequence.
  • Prompt video from Moodle upload, direct URL, YouTube or Vimeo.
  • Text, uploaded audio, uploaded video and browser-recorded responses.
  • Per-question response time limits.
  • One, multiple or unlimited interview attempts.
  • Optional review/edit stage before final submission.
  • Assessment criteria with score, weight and teacher feedback.
  • Moodle gradebook integration.
Progress and reporting

Teacher reports can distinguish started, answered, submitted and evaluated states and include the resulting grade. HTML5 prompt videos can also use viewing-progress and resume information.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Interview supports interviews where the next question or prompt may follow a configured sequence or depend on previous responses. This is useful for structured practice in which learners demonstrate explanations, communication or decision making through text or recorded media. Teachers should map each branch or next step before publication and test what happens when a learner pauses or returns to an unfinished attempt. A clear interview structure helps keep the exercise comparable across participants without eliminating the possibility of different paths.

name: Video Quiz
description: Pause a video at configured moments to ask graded questions while tracking watched segments and completion.
description_html:
Video Quiz

Pause a video at teacher-defined moments, collect answers and combine question performance with real viewing progress.

Questions appear on the timeline

Teachers place questions at specific video positions. Playback pauses automatically at each configured point, the learner answers and receives the configured feedback before continuing according to the activity rules.

Question and video options
  • Multiple choice, true/false, short answer and multiple-answer questions.
  • Mandatory or optional questions.
  • One or multiple attempts per question.
  • Correct and incorrect feedback.
  • Configurable points and optional later answer changes.
  • Uploaded video, direct URL, YouTube and Vimeo.
  • WebVTT captions and poster image for HTML5 sources.
  • Watched-segment tracking and resume playback.
Flexible grading and completion

Grades can be based on questions only, watched percentage only or a configurable combination of both. Moodle completion can require a minimum watched percentage, all mandatory questions, a minimum grade or a combination of those conditions.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Quiz combines scheduled video interruptions with questions, encouraging learners to respond at the moment a concept is being demonstrated. Teachers can choose checkpoints that genuinely require interpreting the preceding scene, rather than inserting arbitrary questions at regular intervals. The resulting activity can connect watched coverage, answers, grades and completion rules, giving a more useful learning checkpoint than playback alone. Teacher review should distinguish performance on the questions from the time spent watching, since they provide different kinds of evidence.

name: BookFlow
description: Interactive book activity with chapters, rich content blocks, reading progress, completion rules, bookmarks, notes, search, reports, import/export, and backup/restore support.
description_html:
BookFlow

Create structured interactive books with chapters, rich content blocks, reading progress, learner notes and completion rules in a single course activity.

Build content from chapters and blocks

BookFlow supports chapters and subchapters containing independent content blocks. Available blocks include HTML, Markdown, callouts, images, video, audio, downloads, code, accordions, tabs, disclosures, flashcards and questions, allowing one reading activity to mix explanation and interaction.

Progress based on what matters

Content blocks can participate in progress with different weights, be ignored for progress, or be marked as required. Chapters can also be required, and the activity supports percentage-based, required-content, combined and required-chapter completion strategies.

Learners can resume from their last chapter and block instead of searching manually for where they stopped.

Tools for active reading
  • Private bookmarks for returning to important places.
  • Private notes attached to the reading experience.
  • Internal search across the book.
  • Flashcards and question blocks alongside regular content.
Content management and reporting

Teachers can reorder content, review student, chapter and content reports, and move material in or out through Standard Book, HTML and Markdown imports plus HTML, Markdown, ZIP and print exports. Activity and learner data can also participate in backup and restore.

Practical use and interpretation

BookFlow is intended for content that should be navigated as a coherent learning flow rather than as unrelated Moodle resources. Teachers can organize reading steps and progression while retaining familiar course context. The strongest use case is a sequence where each section prepares the learner for the next, with navigation that makes the intended path clear. Institutions should verify the workflow on smaller screens and with assistive technologies, and clarify whether the activity is for reading, progress tracking or an assessed task.

name: Agreement
description: Publish a versioned agreement and record an explicit immutable Agree or Disagree decision for audit purposes.
description_html:
Agreement

Publish a policy, declaration or term that requires each participant to record an explicit Agree or Disagree decision against the exact version they received.

More than a viewed flag

Agreement creates an explicit decision record rather than treating page access as acceptance. Each learner response is immutable for that version of the agreement and remains tied to the exact text that was shown.

Changing the agreement text or text format automatically creates a new version. Learners must respond again, while earlier decisions remain preserved with the historical version.

Audit-oriented behavior
  • Explicit Agree or Disagree response.
  • Separate capabilities for responding and read-only viewing.
  • One immutable response per learner and agreement version.
  • Automatic version creation when the agreement content changes.
  • Date and time stored for each decision.
  • SHA-256 content hash for each version.
  • Teacher report for current status, version history and response history.
  • Backup/restore and Moodle Privacy API support.
Suitable for policies and declarations

The versioned model is useful when institutions need to know not only that a learner accepted something, but exactly which wording was presented at the time of the decision.

Practical use and interpretation

Agreement provides a deliberate acceptance step for course policies, expectations or terms that participants need to acknowledge. It helps teachers distinguish merely presenting a document from obtaining an explicit action from a learner. The text should be understandable and versioned according to institutional practice, because an agreement is only useful when people can see what they accepted. Teachers should also explain the consequences of declining or not yet accepting, and avoid treating a recorded click as proof that the participant read every word.

name: Video Prediction
description: Pause video at teacher-defined points and require learners to predict outcomes before playback continues.
description_html:
Video Prediction

Pause a video before important moments and require learners to predict what will happen before the real outcome is revealed.

Prediction before continuation

Teachers create prediction points on the video timeline. At a mandatory point, playback stops and the learner must save the original prediction before continuing, preserving what they thought before seeing the outcome.

A separate reveal time can define when the actual result becomes visible, and an optional reflection can ask learners whether and why their understanding changed.

Prediction formats and playback
  • Open response, multiple choice, true/false and possible-outcome questions.
  • Multiple prediction points in one video.
  • Immutable original predictions after submission.
  • Separate outcome reveal time.
  • Optional post-result reflection.
  • HTML5 upload/direct URL, HLS, YouTube and Vimeo.
  • Watched-segment tracking, resume and seek protection.
  • Timeline markers for prediction points.
Assessment and reporting

Objective predictions can be scored automatically while open responses support teacher grading. Grades can use prediction score, viewing progress or a blended model, and reports show responses, correctness, reflections, viewing progress and whether understanding changed.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Prediction invites learners to pause at a meaningful moment and anticipate what comes next before seeing the outcome. This makes a demonstration more active: the teacher can ask for a hypothesis, then use the following scene as evidence for discussion. Prediction prompts work best where multiple plausible outcomes exist and learners can explain their reasoning. A wrong prediction can be pedagogically useful when it exposes a misconception, so feedback should encourage comparing the prediction with what the video actually shows.

name: Hand Raise
description: Manage a live speaking queue where learners request a turn and teachers mark requests as attended.
description_html:
Hand Raise

Organize requests to speak during live classes and synchronous sessions with a simple first-in, first-out queue.

A queue instead of competing for attention

Learners click the request-to-speak action and enter the queue in arrival order. They can see their own position and cancel the request if they no longer need to speak.

Teachers see the named queue with request time and waiting time and remove participants as they are served.

Live updating workflow
  • First-in, first-out ordering.
  • Learner view of personal position and total queue size.
  • Learner cancellation.
  • Teacher view of participant names, request time and waiting time.
  • Served action for removing the current request.
  • Automatic AJAX refresh without reloading the page.
Privacy-aware student view

Learners do not receive the names of other queued participants through the API. Only users with the queue-management capability can access the named list, making the activity suitable for classrooms, tutoring, webinars and workshops.

Practical use and interpretation

Hand Raise organizes requests for a speaking turn during a live class or synchronous activity. Learners can indicate that they wish to participate, while the teacher manages a visible queue and marks requests as attended. This is useful for reducing interruptions and avoiding the need to remember who asked first. Clear rules for repeated requests, accessibility and how the queue is reset help prevent confusion. It is a facilitation tool, not an attendance record or an automatic measure of participation quality.

name: Trigonometry
description: Provide an interactive browser-based trigonometry calculator with degree, radian and unit-circle views.
description_html:
Trigonometry

Explore sine, cosine, tangent, inverse functions and the unit circle through an interactive calculator inside Moodle.

Calculate and visualize

Learners can enter angles in degrees or radians and calculate sine, cosine and tangent. Inverse sine, cosine and tangent are also available, with results shown in both degree and radian forms where appropriate.

The activity handles the valid domains of inverse sine and cosine and presents common trigonometric identities alongside the interactive calculations.

Interactive unit circle
  • Degree and radian angle input.
  • Sine, cosine and tangent.
  • Arc sine, arc cosine and arc tangent.
  • Inverse-function results in degrees and radians.
  • Interactive unit circle with x/y projections.
  • Tangent visualization.
  • Draggable point and angle slider.
  • Common trigonometric identities and relationships.
A browser-based learning tool

All calculations run locally in the browser. The plugin does not store learner answers, making the activity suitable for guided exploration, demonstrations and practice rather than a submission workflow.

Practical use and interpretation

Trigonometry supplies an interactive space for exploring trigonometric functions, angles and representations such as degrees, radians and the unit circle. Teachers can use it to connect a numeric result to geometric interpretation rather than requiring students to memorize values without context. Learners can vary the angle and compare the corresponding function values and visual position. The tool works best when paired with tasks that ask students to explain periodicity, signs and relationships, not simply enter a value and copy the result.

name: Fractions
description: Simplify, compare and calculate fractions while showing the arithmetic steps used for each result.
description_html:
Fractions

Simplify, compare and calculate with fractions while showing the mathematical steps behind every result.

Fraction operations in one activity

Learners can simplify fractions, compare two fractions, add, subtract, multiply and divide them, or convert between fraction and decimal forms.

The calculator runs in the browser, so entered values are not stored as learner submissions.

Show the reasoning, not only the answer
  • Greatest common divisor using the Euclidean algorithm.
  • Least common multiple for equivalent denominators.
  • Cross multiplication for comparisons.
  • Step-by-step simplification.
  • Addition and subtraction with denominator conversion.
  • Multiplication and division of fractions.
  • Fraction-to-decimal and decimal-to-fraction conversion.
Useful for guided practice

Because the activity exposes the intermediate calculations, it can support classroom explanation and self-practice without behaving like a hidden calculator that returns only a final value.

Features in practice

Fractions is a guided arithmetic tool for simplifying, comparing and calculating rational numbers. Rather than providing only a result, it displays calculation steps so learners can inspect how numerators and denominators are handled. The activity can accompany examples on equivalent fractions, operations involving unlike denominators and simplification of final answers. Teachers can ask learners to predict an intermediate transformation before using the tool to check the arithmetic. This is especially useful for distinguishing a valid common denominator from a merely plausible result. The activity helps verify calculations, but understanding the reasoning still requires explanation and practice.

name: Video Reflection
description: Combine tracked video viewing with timed reflection prompts, learner notes, questions and class analysis.
description_html:
Video Reflection

Combine tracked video viewing with teacher prompts and learner reflections attached to precise moments on the timeline.

Reflect while watching
