Teachers can create general prompts or prompts linked to a specific video time. Learners can also create their own reflections and questions while watching, keeping the reflective process connected to the exact content that triggered it.

Timed prompts and reflections are clickable, allowing the player to jump directly back to the referenced moment.

Video and reflection features
  • Uploaded file, direct media URL, YouTube and Vimeo.
  • Real watched-segment tracking.
  • Configurable resume behavior.
  • General and timestamped teacher prompts.
  • Required prompts for completion.
  • Learner-created reflections and questions.
  • Private or shared-class mode.
  • Completion by watched percentage, reflection count and required prompts.
Reports for metacognitive review

Individual and class reports help teachers see participation and identify video moments that attract the greatest concentration of reflections or questions.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Reflection ties prompts and learner reflections to moments in a video so the response has a visible source. Teachers can ask a question during a demonstration and invite learners to document what they noticed, what surprised them or which decision they would make. Timestamped notes make later review more grounded than a general reaction written after the entire clip. The teacher should specify whether the purpose is private reflection, shared discussion or assessment, because the appropriate feedback workflow differs.

name: Video Lesson
description: Turn one video into a structured chapter-based lesson with independent progress and complementary materials.
description_html:
Video Lesson

Turn one video into a structured lesson with chapters, independent progress and complementary learning material for each stage.

Chapters with their own learning requirements

Teachers divide the video by timecode and can mark chapters as required or optional. Each chapter tracks its own viewing percentage and status, and sequential locking can require one chapter to be completed before the next becomes available.

A chapter can contain complementary text, images, PDFs, files, links, questions or activity guidance, and selected complementary items can themselves be required for chapter completion.

Tracked video lesson features
  • Uploaded video, direct URL/HLS, YouTube and Vimeo.
  • WebVTT captions for HTML5 sources.
  • Per-chapter watched percentage and status.
  • Optional sequential chapter locking.
  • Required and optional chapters.
  • Complementary resources per chapter.
  • Overall lesson progress.
  • Resume from the latest server-validated position.
  • Per-learner and per-chapter progress reporting.
Completion and gradebook

Overall completion can require all mandatory chapters or a configured progress percentage. The overall progress value can also be published to the Moodle gradebook, giving the structured lesson a measurable course-level result.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Lesson brings media into a more structured instructional path, allowing teachers to shape how the learner moves through video-based content rather than publishing one long recording without guidance. The activity is useful for demonstrations, explanatory sequences and lessons that need learner progression to be visible. Teachers should identify the learning objective of each segment, check playback controls on target devices and define completion based on the behavior the activity actually records. A video lesson remains more effective when active questions and tasks accompany the media.

name: Video Marker
description: Ask learners to identify precise moments or intervals in a video and integrate the selections with tracking and grading.
description_html:
Activity module Video
Video Marker

Turn video observation into an assessable activity by asking learners to identify the exact moment or complete interval in which something happens.

Video Marker is designed for learning activities where understanding when an event occurs is part of the objective. Instead of answering only with text or multiple choice, the learner watches the video and places markers directly on its timeline.

Point and interval questions

Teachers can create different kinds of temporal questions depending on what learners need to recognise in the video.

  • Point questions: the learner marks one precise moment, such as when an error, action, symptom or important event first occurs.
  • Interval questions: the learner marks the complete beginning and end of a segment, such as the full duration of an incorrect procedure.
  • Multiple markers: a question can require more than one point or interval when the same event appears several times.

For point questions, the teacher can define a correctness window around the expected second. For interval questions, expected start and end boundaries can use configurable tolerance. This makes grading suitable for real video observation, where a small temporal difference should not necessarily make an otherwise correct answer wrong.

Automatic evaluation and feedback

The activity compares the learner's submitted markers with the expected positions configured by the teacher. It can record whether each answer is correct, how far the marker is from the expected target, the resulting grade and completion of required questions.

Retry and feedback behaviour can be configured per question, allowing the activity to be used both for formative practice and for graded observation exercises.

Video progress is part of the activity

Video Marker also tracks viewing progress. The learner can resume playback from where they stopped, while the activity records watched percentage together with the marker answers. This allows completion rules to consider both the required questions and actual engagement with the video.

Supported video sources
  • Protected Moodle video upload.
  • Direct video URL.
  • YouTube.
  • Vimeo.
Teacher review

Teachers can review attempts with the learner's markers, marker accuracy, grades, watched percentage and completion status. This provides more useful evidence than a simple correct/incorrect result and helps identify whether a learner recognised the right event but selected it slightly too early or too late.

Useful for observation-based learning

Video Marker is especially useful when learners need to recognise events in sequence or detect evidence inside audiovisual material, including procedural training, safety analysis, sports technique, clinical observation, teacher education, language analysis and media studies.

name: Probability Simulator
description: Simulate coins, dice and configurable urn outcomes and compare observed frequencies with theoretical probability.
description_html:
Probability Simulator

Compare theoretical probability with observed frequency by running repeated simulations directly in the browser.

Run the same experiment many times

Learners choose an experiment and run 10, 100 or 1,000 trials. The activity compares the simulated distribution with the theoretical probability so learners can see how observed frequency behaves as the number of repetitions grows.

Simulation results are calculated in the browser and individual runs are not stored.

Included experiments
  • Coin with a configurable probability of heads.
  • Die with between 2 and 100 sides.
  • Urn with any number of named outcomes and configurable quantities.
Useful for probability intuition

The activity supports demonstrations and practice around expected probability, random variation and the relationship between small samples and larger numbers of trials.

Features in practice

Probability Simulator supports interactive experiments with coins, dice and configurable urn outcomes. Learners can repeat trials, compare observed counts and percentages with theoretical probabilities and see how sample variation appears in different runs. In a lesson, a teacher can begin with a small number of trials and then increase the sample to discuss why relative frequencies often stabilize over time. The tool is useful for connecting abstract probability models to observable results without manually repeating hundreds of physical throws or draws. Simulations rely on the selected mathematical assumptions, so their outcomes should not be confused with a guarantee about every real-world process.

name: Subcourse
description: Use the final grade from another Moodle course as the grade of an activity in the current course.
description_html:
Subcourse

Use the final grade from another Moodle course as the grade for an activity in the current course.

Connect course structures through grades

Subcourse behaves like a graded activity inside the main course, but its learner grade is taken from the final grade of a referenced course.

This allows course designers to split a larger learning program into separate Moodle courses while still representing the result of each referenced course inside the main course.

Typical workflow
  • Create a main course and one or more courses that act as subcourses.
  • Add a Subcourse activity in the main course for each referenced course.
  • Enroll learners in both the main course and the referenced courses.
  • Let learners complete the referenced course normally.
  • Use the referenced course final grade as the grade shown by the Subcourse activity.
Useful for modular course design

Subcourse is useful when a curriculum is intentionally divided into reusable course units but the parent course still needs one activity-level result representing each unit.

Practical use and interpretation

Subcourse links progress or grades from another Moodle course into a parent course, which can reduce administrative duplication in programs that share a common component. The important design choice is which external result should count in the parent, and how it should behave when a learner has not yet completed the source course. Institutions should review enrolment and synchronization semantics before using this for high-stakes grade calculation. A linked grade reflects a defined external source; it should not be treated as independent evidence.

name: Traffic Light
description: Collect a quick green, yellow or red understanding signal from learners during class.
description_html:
Traffic Light

Give learners a fast way to tell the teacher whether they understand, are unsure or need help.

A current-state classroom signal

Learners choose one of three states: green when they understand and are following well, yellow when they have doubts or need review, and red when they need help or do not understand.

Each learner keeps only one current response. If the learner changes state, the previous value is replaced so the dashboard reflects the present situation rather than building a response history.

Teacher dashboard
  • Current totals for green, yellow and red.
  • Percentages for each state.
  • Learners grouped by their selected status.
  • A view of who has not responded yet.
  • Immediate class-level feedback without requiring a graded quiz or long form.
Useful during live teaching

Traffic Light can be used while explaining a topic, after an exercise or before moving to the next part of a lesson. It gives the teacher a quick signal for deciding whether to continue, review or provide targeted help.

Practical use and interpretation

Traffic Light gives learners a fast way to indicate their perceived understanding using an intuitive red, amber or green signal. Teachers can use the distribution during a lesson to decide whether to review a topic or continue. The strength of the activity is immediacy: participants do not need to fill out a long survey to communicate uncertainty. These responses are self-assessments, however, and should be compared with exercises or discussion before drawing conclusions about mastery.

name: Video Peer Review
description: Collect timestamped video feedback and criterion-based teacher or peer assessment.
description_html:
Video Peer Review

Collect timestamped feedback and criterion-based assessment on a common video or on videos submitted by learners.

Two review models

Teachers can publish one common video for the class to evaluate or allow every learner to submit a video that will be reviewed by the teacher and/or assigned peers.

Comments are timestamped, so reviewers can point to an exact moment and later jump directly back to that part of the video.

Peer-review workflow
  • Common-video and learner-submission modes.
  • Uploaded video, direct URL, YouTube and Vimeo.
  • Timestamped comments with click-to-seek navigation.
  • Numeric and concept-based criteria.
  • Optional feedback for each criterion.
  • Automatic peer allocation with configurable reviews per learner.
  • Anonymous peer display for learners while teachers retain audit visibility.
  • Optional delayed release of received reviews.
Progress, grades and reports

The activity records viewing progress per evaluator and reviewed video. Reports cover reviews received, reviews performed, progress and grades, while learner-submission mode can publish grades to the Moodle gradebook and use completion rules for submission and assigned reviews.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Peer Review uses a recording as the object of structured feedback between learners. Teachers can ask participants to observe a performance, choose evidence-based comments and review peers' work against specified expectations. A good peer-review prompt directs attention to particular criteria instead of simply asking whether the video was 'good'. Access permissions, deadlines and the distinction between peer comments and teacher grading should be explained clearly so learners know how their contributions will be used.

name: Quick Decision
description: Run fast single-choice decisions where there is no correct answer and results visibility is configurable.
description_html:
Quick Decision

Run a fast single-choice decision where there is no correct answer and the goal is preference, prioritization or consensus.

One question, several alternatives

The teacher creates one question with two or more options. Each learner keeps one current response and can change it while the activity is open when the teacher allows changes.

Typical uses include choosing the next topic, selecting a meeting time, prioritizing projects or checking the group's preferred direction.

Control when results appear
  • Results can remain hidden.
  • Results can appear after the learner votes.
  • Results can remain visible throughout the activity.
  • Results can become visible only after the activity closes.
  • Learners can be allowed or prevented from changing their choice.
Designed for decisions, not assessment

Quick Decision does not assume one answer is correct. It provides a compact decision workflow for situations where the class needs to choose, prioritize or reveal preferences.

Practical use and interpretation

Quick Decision collects a fast choice among alternatives when the objective is to discover preferences or reach a class decision, not mark answers right or wrong. Teachers can pose a question, configure when results are visible and invite participants to select an option. The pattern is useful for choosing discussion topics, checking opinions or making a simple collective decision. Visibility rules matter: showing early responses can influence later choices, so teachers should select the reporting behavior deliberately.

name: Class Pulse
description: Collect a quick classroom understanding signal and display aggregated live charts to the teacher.
description_html:
Class Pulse

Collect a fast signal of learner understanding and watch the class distribution update while a lesson is in progress.

Four levels of understanding

The default options range from not understanding through partial understanding to understanding and mastery. Teachers can use the activity as a low-friction check during or after an explanation.

Learners may be allowed or prevented from changing their response, depending on whether the teacher wants a fixed snapshot or a continuously updated pulse.

Live aggregate report
  • Automatic report refresh while the dashboard is open.
  • Pie, bar and line chart views.
  • Anonymous or identified mode.
  • Teacher-configurable question.
  • Teacher-configurable response-change policy.
Anonymous mode with duplicate protection

When anonymous mode is enabled, the learner id is stored as zero. The activity uses an activity-specific HMAC SHA-256 value only to prevent duplicate responses, while the teacher dashboard receives aggregate counts rather than that identifier.

Practical use and interpretation

Class Pulse collects a brief understanding signal and displays aggregated live results for the teacher. It can support a momentary check during a difficult explanation or before moving on to a new concept. Teachers can ask a clear question and use the distribution to decide whether additional examples are needed. A signal is valuable for adapting teaching in the moment, but should not be confused with a graded assessment or long-term evidence of what each learner has mastered.

name: Ohm's Law
description: Calculate voltage, current, resistance and power from any two positive known quantities and show the steps.
description_html:
Ohm's Law

Calculate voltage, current, resistance and power from any two known positive quantities and show the relationships used to obtain the result.

Enter any two known values

Learners provide any two positive values among voltage, current, resistance and power. The calculator immediately derives the remaining two quantities directly in the browser.

Alongside the final values, the activity shows the calculation steps and the equivalent relationships used between V, I, R and P.

Additional electrical relationships
  • Voltage, current, resistance and power calculation.
  • Automatic derivation from any valid pair of known quantities.
  • Visible calculation steps.
  • Equivalent V/I/R/P relationships.
  • Conductance.
  • Common electrical unit conversions.
Practice without stored answers

Learner-entered values are not stored. The activity can therefore be used as a guided classroom calculator and as a visual aid for exploring how the core electrical quantities relate to one another.

Practical use and interpretation

Ohm's Law helps learners calculate voltage, current, resistance and power from suitable known values, with the intermediate reasoning shown alongside the result. It can support electronics exercises in which students need to understand how changing one quantity affects another. Teachers can ask for predictions and then compare the calculator's result with algebraic work. The activity assumes the relationships of the chosen electrical model and positive valid inputs; students should still verify units and whether the physical scenario matches those assumptions.

name: Video Diagnostic
description: Capture a pre-study diagnosis from video, release explanations and compare the learner's initial and later responses.
description_html:
Main features
Before-and-after diagnosis

Collect an initial response before the explanation is shown and optionally ask the same diagnostic questions again after the study stage.

Multiple question formats

Use open responses, choices, video moments and video intervals so the diagnostic can measure both conceptual answers and evidence tied to the timeline.

Explanation stage

Provide an optional explanatory video, solution, teacher comments and complementary materials between the initial and final responses.

Automatic comparison

The activity compares initial and final answers so teachers can see how the learner's diagnosis changed after studying the explanation.

Optional diagnostic scoring

Expected answers, expected choices and expected video ranges can be used for automatic scoring; when no automatic criterion exists, the activity remains diagnostic-only.

Class and learner reports

Reports include selected timecodes, answer evolution, watched progress and CSV export.

Supported sources
Moodle upload Direct video URL YouTube Vimeo
Moodle integration
  • Server-side watched-segment tracking with unique watched percentage.
  • Large playback discontinuities are not counted as watched content.
  • Custom completion can require the initial submission and/or a watched percentage.
  • Backup and restore support, including user data when requested.
  • Moodle Privacy API support.
  • Diagnostic scores remain inside the activity and do not create a Moodle gradebook item.
Why this activity exists

Video Diagnostic foi pensado para diagnóstico de conhecimento prévio e mudança conceitual. O estudante responde antes da explicação, recebe a etapa de estudo e, quando habilitado, responde novamente às mesmas questões, permitindo comparar o raciocínio inicial com o que mudou depois do contato com o conteúdo.

Learning flow
1. Initial diagnostic

The learner watches the initial situation and answers before the explanatory material is released.

2. Baseline is preserved

The first response remains stored as the original diagnostic evidence.

3. Study stage is released

The activity can show an explanatory video, solution, teacher comments and complementary material.

4. Post-study comparison

A second response can be collected and compared directly with the initial one.

What learners can do
Open response

Capture the learner diagnosis or explanation in their own words.

Choice question

Use structured alternatives when the diagnostic requires a specific decision.

Video moment

Ask the learner to select the exact instant that supports the diagnosis.

Video interval

Capture evidence that spans a start and end point in the timeline.

Expected answers

Automatic criteria can be configured for text, options or expected video ranges when appropriate.

Diagnostic-only mode

When no automatic criterion exists, the activity remains diagnostic instead of manufacturing a grade.

Tracking and evidence

The activity periodically submits the real playback position and small contiguous watched intervals. The server merges accepted segments and calculates unique watched time and percentage, while large discontinuities are not accepted as watched content. This prevents a simple seek-to-end action from appearing as complete viewing.

Teacher reports
Initial response

Keep the answer submitted before study as the diagnostic baseline.

Final response

Show the post-study answer when the second response is enabled.

Answer evolution

Compare both responses side by side to make conceptual change visible.

Timecode evidence

Moment and interval selections remain attached to the learner response.

Class overview

Identify recurring misconceptions and patterns across learners.

CSV export

Export structured diagnostic data for further analysis.

Typical uses
Prior-knowledge assessmentMisconception analysisClinical reasoningCase diagnosisConceptual changeFormative assessment

name: Video Playlist
description: Place multiple trackable videos in one activity with per-video progress, sequential unlocking and overall completion.
description_html:
Video Playlist

Combine multiple trackable videos in one Moodle activity and calculate progress across the entire playlist.

Multiple videos, one learning activity

Teachers build a playlist of videos while the plugin tracks each video independently. Learners can resume individual videos from their saved positions and see progress across the full collection.

Sequential unlocking can require a minimum watched percentage in one video before the next video becomes available.

Tracking and progression
  • Multiple videos per activity.
  • Moodle upload, direct URL/HLS, YouTube and Vimeo.
  • Per-video watched-segment tracking.
  • Per-video resume position and percentage.
  • Optional sequential unlocking.
  • Overall progress calculated as the arithmetic mean of enabled videos.
  • Custom completion rule based on overall percentage.
  • Gradebook integration using overall percentage.
Teacher management and reports

The plugin includes a management interface for the playlist and a report showing progress per learner and per video, making it suitable for video series, microlearning collections and structured viewing sequences.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Playlist gathers multiple videos in one learning activity while retaining progress at the item level. Teachers can configure whether videos are released sequentially and how the collection contributes to completion. This is useful for a multi-part course explanation or a series of practical demonstrations, where students benefit from seeing the order and their remaining items. Playlist progression should distinguish opening a clip from actually meeting its tracked viewing requirement, and course teams should test the configured unlocking behavior.

name: Mood Tracker
description: Collect one quick learner mood check-in per activity and give teachers an aggregated class view without turning the activity into a long survey.
description_html:
Class pulseAggregated dashboard

Mood Tracker

Ask learners for a quick mood signal and give the teacher a class-level view that can be checked during or between learning activities.

Each learner selects one mood from a small configured set, with an option controlling whether they may change the response after submission.

Focused by design
  • One simple mood response per learner/activity.
  • Aggregated teacher dashboard.
  • Capability-controlled reporting.
  • Stored response covered by Moodle privacy handling.
Features in practice

Mood Tracker offers a brief learner check-in with five predefined mood choices and a teacher dashboard that reports the distribution in aggregate. Teachers can decide whether the first submission remains fixed or whether learners may change their answer, in which case the current response replaces the previous one. Reports include participant counts and pending responses, making the activity useful before a lesson, after a challenge or as an occasional class pulse. Individual choices are not presented publicly to classmates. A self-reported mood represents a momentary perception, not a diagnosis or an evaluation of a learner's intelligence, effort or academic progress.

Practical use and interpretation

The dashboard is most helpful when the teacher interprets changes across sessions alongside what is happening in class, rather than labeling individual students from one check-in. An unexpectedly large number of pending responses may simply mean that some learners were absent or had not opened the activity. The visible aggregate is designed to guide conversation and course support, not clinical evaluation.

name: One-minute Paper
description: Collect a concise one-minute-paper response with optional dates, IP/geolocation restrictions and CSV reporting.
description_html:
One-minute Paper

Use the classic one-minute paper technique to collect a short learner reflection with optional time and presence controls.

A focused reflection prompt

Teachers define a short prompt, response limit and optional opening and closing dates. Each participant keeps one editable response while the activity is open.

The technique works well for questions such as the main concept learned, the most important takeaway or the point that remains unclear.

Teacher review and export
  • One response per learner.
  • Editable response while the activity remains open.
  • Group-aware teacher report.
  • CSV export.
  • Configurable response limit.
  • Optional opening and closing dates.
Optional presence validation

Responses can optionally be restricted to the same detected public IP as the teacher or to a geographic radius around a teacher reference point, supporting classroom use when a simple presence signal is desirable.

Practical use and interpretation

One-minute Paper captures a concise written reflection or response before learners leave a session. It is useful for asking what was most important, which question remains unanswered or how someone would summarize a concept. Teachers can quickly review recurring themes and adjust the next lesson accordingly, while CSV reporting supports further analysis when authorized. The learning value comes from acting on that feedback and keeping prompts focused, rather than turning a short reflection into an unnecessarily complex assessment.

name: Matrix Calculator
description: Work with matrix addition, multiplication, determinant, transpose and inverse while showing calculation steps.
description_html:
Matrix Calculator

Work with matrices directly inside Moodle and show the calculation process instead of returning only a final matrix.

Interactive matrix operations

Learners define the dimensions of matrices A and B, enter their values and choose one of the operations enabled by the teacher. The activity performs the calculation in the browser and presents step-by-step details for the result.

Available operations
  • Matrix addition.
  • Matrix multiplication.
  • Determinant using Gaussian elimination.
  • Transpose of matrix A or B.
  • Inverse using Gauss-Jordan elimination.
  • Support for row and column vectors when the selected operation permits them.
  • Teacher-controlled operation list.
  • Configurable maximum dimension from 2 to 8.
No stored calculation history

Values entered by learners are processed locally in the browser and are not stored by the plugin, making the activity suitable for demonstrations and guided practice.

Practical use and interpretation

Matrix Calculator supports common matrix operations such as addition, multiplication, transpose, determinant and inverse, showing computational steps where applicable. Teachers can use it to check intermediate algebra during linear algebra lessons, while learners change input values and observe how the results respond. Particular attention should be given to dimension compatibility and singular matrices, because these conditions determine whether an operation makes sense. The calculator is a numerical learning aid and does not remove the need to understand the underlying rules.

name: Percentage Calculator
description: Calculate and visualize percentages, variation, increases, discounts, margin, markup and profit.
description_html:
Percentage Calculator

Calculate and visualize percentages so learners can see both the numeric result and its proportional meaning.

Several percentage problems in one activity
  • Percentage of a value.
  • Percentage represented by a part of a total.
  • Percentage change between initial and final values.
  • Percentage increase.
  • Percentage discount.
  • Margin, markup and profit.
Visual representations

Results can be shown as a proportional bar, donut chart, 10 × 10 percentage grid or before/after comparison. The activity can also choose a suitable visualization automatically according to the calculation type.

Teacher-controlled learning aid

Teachers choose which calculations are available, define the default visualization, set decimal precision and decide whether the formula and explanatory text appear with the answer. This makes the activity useful for mathematics, finance and business contexts where understanding the relationship matters as much as the result.

Practical use and interpretation

Percentage Calculator makes percentage calculations and commercial applications easier to inspect, including variation, increases, discounts, margin, markup and profit. In practical exercises, learners can change the base value or rate and see how the result changes, then compare it with a manual calculation. Teachers should emphasize which value serves as the base in each scenario, since many percentage errors come from choosing the wrong reference amount. A computed percentage is a starting point for interpreting a financial or statistical statement, not a complete explanation.

name: Video Notes
description: Combine tracked video playback with private timestamped learner notes, categories, search and exports.
description_html:
Video Notes

Let learners create private notes tied to exact video timestamps and return to those moments instantly.

Notes connected to playback

Learners write notes while watching and each note keeps the current video position. Clicking a note seeks the player back to that exact moment, turning the note list into a personal index of the video.

Notes are private by default, while individual notes can optionally be shared with teachers.

Note and video features
  • Moodle upload, direct URL, YouTube and Vimeo.
  • Watched progress based on segments actually played.
  • Resume from the latest playback position.
  • Important, Question, Review and Example note categories.
  • Timestamped click-to-seek notes.
  • Search across the learner's own notes.
  • Print, CSV export and text export.
  • Optional per-note sharing with teachers.
Completion and teacher visibility

Completion can require a minimum number of notes, a minimum watched percentage or both. Teacher reports include only notes the learner explicitly chose to share.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Notes gives learners a private note-taking space anchored to playback timestamps. Rather than trying to find a sentence in an unrelated notebook, participants can return to the associated moment while reviewing a lesson. Categories and search make repeated notes easier to manage, and export supports revision outside the activity. Teachers can encourage note quality by asking students to record concepts, questions or examples instead of transcribing the entire recording. Private notes remain study material rather than publicly visible forum contributions.

name: Chat
description: Provide real-time text discussions inside a Moodle course.
description_html:
Chat

Provide a synchronous text-based discussion space inside a Moodle course for live class conversation and group interaction.

Real-time course discussion

The Chat activity gives course participants a shared text space for synchronous communication. It can support virtual class discussions, live question sessions, group work and other situations where participants need to exchange messages at the same time.

Because the activity lives inside the Moodle course, access follows the course context rather than requiring a separate messaging service.

Simple synchronous interaction

Learners enter the activity during the planned session and participate in a text conversation with the other users who have access. The activity is intended for real-time use rather than asynchronous forum-style discussion.

When to use it

Chat is useful when a course needs a lightweight, course-contained live text channel. For institutions that need a broader modern messaging stack, Moodle's Matrix integration may be a better fit, but Chat remains a straightforward activity for synchronous text sessions.

Practical use and interpretation

Chat offers text-based course conversation within Moodle's activity structure. It can support synchronous questions, collaborative problem-solving or a scheduled discussion without requiring participants to join a separate messaging platform. Teachers should communicate expected availability, moderation and whether the conversation is part of a formal lesson. A chat works best when the topic is specific and participants can follow the exchange; it is less suitable for long-lived structured resources that belong in forums or course pages.

name: Video Observation
description: Perform systematic video observation using teacher-defined events, timestamps, intervals and aggregate reports.
description_html:
Main features
Teacher-defined observation sheet

Teachers create reusable event types describing what learners should identify while watching the video.

Moment and interval observations

Students can mark a single instant or an interval and optionally add a textual note to explain what they observed.

Teacher reference observations

Teachers can register expected moments or intervals and compare learner marks against the reference using a configurable tolerance.

Aggregate analysis

Reports include event frequencies, time clusters, differences between learners, average markings and matches against the teacher reference.

Final observation sheet

The activity automatically consolidates the learner's markings into a final sheet and timeline.

Viewing progress

Watched segments and the last playback position are tracked alongside the observation data.

Supported sources
Moodle upload Direct video URL YouTube Vimeo
How it works
  1. Create the activity and select the video source.
  2. Create the event types in the observation sheet.
  3. Optionally register teacher reference observations.
  4. Learners watch the video and mark occurrences.
  5. Use the aggregate report to compare frequencies, time clusters, learners and reference matches.
Moodle integration
  • Uploaded videos and poster images are served through Moodle File API.
  • Custom completion can use watched percentage and number of observations.
  • Requires Moodle 4.4 or later.
Why this activity exists

Video Observation transforma observação audiovisual em dados estruturados. O professor define uma ficha com tipos de evento reutilizáveis e o estudante registra cada ocorrência no momento ou intervalo correspondente, podendo adicionar uma nota e depois comparar seu resultado com padrões da turma ou uma referência do professor.

Learning flow
1. Observation sheet

The teacher defines the events learners should identify.

2. Optional teacher reference

Expected moments or intervals can be recorded as a comparison baseline.

3. Learners mark occurrences

The same event can be registered repeatedly with point or interval evidence.

4. Aggregate analysis

The report compares frequencies, time clusters, learner differences and reference matches.

What learners can do
Reusable event types

Create named categories that define what learners should observe.

Point occurrence

Mark an event at one exact moment.

Interval occurrence

Represent events that span a period.

Optional notes

Add interpretation or context to each observation.

Teacher reference

Record expected observations separately from learner data.

Tolerance window

Define how close a learner mark must be to a reference mark to count as a match.

Tracking and evidence

Watched segments and the latest playback position are stored together with observation marks. This allows the teacher to separate a learner who watched little of the video from one who watched extensively but identified different events. Every observation also preserves its exact moment or interval.

Teacher reports
Final observation sheet

Review the learner complete set of observations.

Event frequency

Count how often each event type was identified.

Time clusters

Find moments where many learners placed observations.

Learner differences

Compare quantity and distribution of marks between students.

Reference matches

Review matches, missed expected marks and extra observations.

Completion

Require a minimum number of observations and/or watched percentage.

Typical uses
Classroom observationSports analysisClinical observationBehavior codingResearch analysisProcedure review

name: Topic Choice
description: Allocate seminar, project, laboratory or presentation topics with fixed capacities and concurrency-safe selection.
description_html:
Topic Choice

Let learners choose seminar, project, laboratory or presentation topics while enforcing the capacity of each option.

Self-service selection with limited places

Teachers create the available topics and set the maximum number of learners for each one. Learners choose while places remain, and a topic automatically stops accepting new selections when its capacity is full.

Moodle's Lock API protects the final available place so two learners cannot claim it at the same time.

Teacher controls
  • Configurable topic names.
  • Individual capacity per topic.
  • Opening and closing dates.
  • Optional learner choice changes.
  • Real-time report of capacity and occupied places.
  • List of learners assigned to each topic.
  • Optional activity completion after a topic is selected.
Useful for constrained allocations

Topic Choice fits project themes, seminar subjects, lab groups and presentation slots where participants should choose for themselves but each option has a limited number of places.

Practical use and interpretation

Topic Choice handles selection among subjects with capacity limits, which is common for seminars, project assignments, laboratory groups and presentations. Learners see permitted options and select a topic without the teacher manually maintaining a shared spreadsheet. When multiple students choose at once, concurrency-safe allocation matters because the interface must not silently overbook a full option. Teachers should set a clear deadline, explain whether selections can be changed and provide a fallback for learners who do not secure their first choice.

name: Financial Calculator
description: Teach financial mathematics with browser-based calculators for simple and compound interest, present/future value and Price-system installments, including formulas and steps.
description_html:
Financial mathematicsCalculation steps

Financial Calculator

Use calculation as a teaching aid by showing the formula and the intermediate steps, not just the final number.

Teachers choose which modes are available in the activity: simple interest, compound interest, present value, future value and fixed installments using the Price system.

Learner workflow
  • Enter the financial values in the browser.
  • Validate inputs before calculation.
  • See localized results, formulas and calculation steps.
  • No learner calculation history is stored by the activity.
Features in practice

Financial Calculator places finance mathematics directly in a Moodle course with simple and compound interest, present and future value and fixed Price-system installments. Teachers can configure which calculation modes are available for the current lesson, and learners enter values to see both the resulting amount and the formula steps. This makes it useful for exploring how rates, payment periods and principal values affect different scenarios, while comparing the calculator with handwritten exercises. Calculations run in the browser and are not stored as personal learning histories. The activity is an educational calculation aid, not investment advice or a substitute for understanding the financial assumptions.

Practical use and interpretation

A useful classroom comparison is to hold the principal fixed while changing the rate or term, then discuss why the accumulated amount or installment changes. Showing the formula beside the result can expose rounding assumptions that a bare currency figure would conceal. Teachers can pair the activity with exercises where students must interpret the answer, because computing a payment and deciding whether a financial arrangement is suitable are different tasks.

name: Video Error Hunt
description: Ask learners to identify expected errors inside a video, explain what they observed and receive configurable scoring.
description_html:
Video Error Hunt

Ask learners to identify errors inside a video by marking the exact moment and explaining what they observed.

Expected errors defined by the teacher

Teachers configure expected errors as time ranges and assign points to each one. While watching, learners use the error-mark action and explain the issue they identified.

The activity records the current timestamp, checks whether it falls inside an expected range and prevents the same expected error from receiving duplicate credit.

Scoring and playback controls
  • Moodle upload, direct URL, YouTube and Vimeo.
  • Real watched-segment tracking, watch time and resume position.
  • Optional seek restriction to watched regions.
  • Expected error ranges with descriptions, order and individual points.
  • Configurable maximum number of learner marks.
  • Optional penalty for incorrect marks.
  • Immediate feedback or feedback only after final submission.
  • Clickable learner timeline with watched segments and error marks.
Teacher reporting

Reports combine watched percentage, found and missed errors, incorrect marks, score, grade and submission status. Class-level information can also reveal which expected errors were hardest for learners to detect.

Practical use and interpretation

Video Error Hunt asks learners to spot mistakes or problematic moments in a recording, encouraging careful observation instead of passive playback. Teachers can embed deliberate errors in a demonstration and challenge students to identify their location and explain what should have happened. This is useful for troubleshooting practice and professional training where recognizing a flawed procedure matters. The quality of the exercise depends on providing clear evidence and feedback, so accidental ambiguity does not reward guessing over genuine analysis.

name: My Status
description: Let each learner maintain one current classroom status while the teacher sees a live grouped dashboard.
description_html:
My Status

Let each learner show their current working state so teachers can monitor a practical class at a glance.

One current state per learner

Teachers define the statuses that make sense for the activity, such as not started, working, need help and finished. Learners select the state that best reflects where they are right now.

Changing the selection replaces the previous value instead of creating a history, keeping the dashboard focused on the current situation.

Teacher dashboard
  • Learners grouped by current status.
  • Separate view for learners who have not selected anything.
  • Automatic dashboard refresh every five seconds.
  • Fast visibility into who is progressing, blocked or requesting help.
Useful for practical sessions

My Status is suited to labs, workshops, exercises and other classes where the teacher needs a live overview of learner progress without interrupting everyone individually.

Practical use and interpretation

My Status provides a simple learner-controlled state for a classroom workflow, while a teacher dashboard groups the current responses for a quick overview. It can help coordinate activities where learners need to indicate whether they are ready, working or awaiting assistance. Since the value represents the learner's current selection, teachers should not interpret it as a permanent history of performance. Clear labels and expectations help participants use the status consistently.

name: Completion Board
description: Let learners mark real-world tasks complete and allow teachers to validate completion from a centralized report.
description_html:
Completion Board

Track real-world tasks that do not need a file submission and optionally require teacher validation before Moodle considers them complete.

Student mark, teacher validation or both

Learners open the activity and mark the real-world task as completed. Teachers review those declarations from a centralized report and can validate the completion when the configured workflow requires it.

Moodle activity completion can be based on the learner mark, teacher validation or the combination of both.

Simple workflow
  • Teacher creates the Completion Board activity.
  • Learner marks the task as completed.
  • Teacher reviews learner declarations in one report.
  • Teacher validates completion when required.
  • Moodle completion reflects the configured validation model.
Designed for offline and practical work

Typical uses include laboratory work, in-person demonstrations, equipment setup, practical attendance checkpoints and tasks performed outside Moodle where the course needs acknowledgement and validation rather than an uploaded file.

Practical use and interpretation

Completion Board lets participants mark real-world tasks as completed and gives teachers a central interface for validation. It is useful where work happens partly outside Moodle but the course still needs a visible progress record. Teachers should define the evidence required for validation and distinguish a self-reported action from a staff-confirmed result. Clear status changes can reduce repeated follow-up messages, while a review workflow protects against treating every unchecked claim as verified achievement.

name: Rubric Assistant
description: Create, review and safely apply Moodle rubrics and marking guides with AI-assisted analysis and explicit teacher control.
description_html:
AI-assisted grading designMoodle 4.5+

Rubric Assistant

Create or review advanced grading criteria from the assignment context while keeping every final grading-form decision in the teacher's hands.

Supported scope
Rubric and Marking guide
Design focus
Human-in-the-loop changes
Built as a Moodle plugin first: permissions, native APIs and human review remain part of the workflow instead of being replaced by an external black box.
Practical results
Production-minded
✓
Draft from real context
Uses the assignment statement, linked competencies, learning objectives and teacher notes to prepare grading-form proposals.
✓
Compare before applying
Shows proposed additions and changes criterion by criterion so the teacher can select and edit only what should be used.
✓
Native Moodle APIs
Reads and writes advanced grading forms through Moodle controllers instead of patching core or updating grading tables directly.
Teacher remains authoritative
AI never saves a rubric by itself and never calculates student grades.
Minimal AI payload
Student submissions, identities, grades and files are not sent to the AI review.
Review before applying
Teachers decide which suggested grading changes to keep or reject.
What this plugin does

Rubric Assistant turns the assignment itself into the starting point for grading-form design. It can draft criteria, review an existing rubric or marking guide, detect overlap and vague wording, and suggest where levels or score proportions deserve attention.

Every proposal is temporary until a teacher reviews it. Existing criteria that are not selected are preserved, structural changes that may require regrading require an additional confirmation, and unsupported grading methods are never switched automatically.

Features you get
Create grading-form drafts
Build a starting rubric or marking guide from assignment goals and context.
Review existing criteria
Look for ambiguity, duplicated intent, weak progression between levels and missing assessment coverage.
Selective application
Accept, reject or edit each proposed criterion independently.
Strict response validation
Reject malformed JSON, invalid source IDs, duplicate scores and other unsafe AI output.
Session-only drafts
Keep proposals temporary rather than creating a second persistent grading store.
Regrading awareness
Require explicit confirmation when a structural change can affect existing grading instances.

Also requires AI Bridge.

name: Course Audit
description: Audit course structure, dates, completion, assessment, content and pedagogy with deterministic rules first and AI only where semantics are needed.
description_html:
Course linterMoodle 4.5+

Course Audit

Run a practical course audit that separates objective Moodle problems from semantic or pedagogical observations instead of asking an LLM to guess everything.

Supported scope
Structure, dates, completion, assessment, content
Design focus
Deterministic checks first
Built as a Moodle plugin first: permissions, native APIs and human review remain part of the workflow instead of being replaced by an external black box.
Practical results
Production-minded
✓
Objective errors stay objective
PHP checks Moodle data for structural, date, completion, grading, link and basic accessibility problems.
✓
AI only for semantics
Pedagogical coherence, unclear instructions and semantic repetition are analysed only after local checks are complete.
✓
No automatic fixes
The report is diagnostic; teachers decide what to change and use Moodle's normal editing screens.
Privacy by design
Learner identities, submissions, grades and private data are excluded from the AI snapshot.
Safe link handling
Authored URLs are validated locally without turning the audit into an outbound-request or SSRF mechanism.
Reusable reports
A content hash avoids repeating successful AI work when the audited course state has not changed.
What this plugin does

Course Audit works like a linter for Moodle courses. It checks empty sections, hidden items, invalid availability data, date inconsistencies, completion setup, grade-item relationships, duplicated authored content, basic accessibility issues and internal links with deterministic rules.

When semantic analysis is enabled, only the normalized course context needed for interpretation is sent for AI analysis. AI findings are kept separate from objective errors and cannot promote a subjective model opinion into a deterministic ERROR.

Features you get
Complete or structure-only modes
Run deterministic checks alone or combine them with semantic analysis.
Section filtering
Limit the snapshot and report to the part of the course currently being reviewed.
Grouped findings
Organize findings by structure, dates, completion, assessment, content, pedagogy, accessibility and links.
Direct edit links
Take the teacher from a finding back to the Moodle item that can actually be changed.
AI failure tolerance
Keep deterministic results available even when the AI route, credits or provider fail.
Content-hash cache
Reuse only successful reports for the same course, user, mode, section and audited content.

Also requires AI Bridge.

name: GeniAI Course Builder
description: Turn a teacher prompt and source files into native Moodle activities through an extensible activity-subplugin architecture.
description_html:
AI course creationMoodle 4.5+

GeniAI Course Builder

Start with a prompt and source files, let specialized subplugins analyse what each source can become, then create real Moodle activities instead of a proprietary course format.

Supported scope
Prompt + multiple source files
Design focus
Native Moodle activities
Built as a Moodle plugin first: permissions, native APIs and human review remain part of the workflow instead of being replaced by an external black box.
Practical results
Production-minded
✓
Specialized activity builders
Each activity subplugin decides whether it can handle the source and owns the logic for creating that Moodle activity.
✓
Teacher chooses the result
The system proposes suitable outputs, but the teacher chooses the final activity type before anything is created.
✓
Extensible architecture
New builders can be added without concentrating every content type and generation rule in the parent plugin.
Native output
Creates standard Moodle activities such as Page, Forum, Quiz, Lesson, Assignment and H5P activities.
Source-aware workflow
Uploaded material is extracted and analysed together with the teacher's instruction for that file.
Central AI integration
Generation is delegated through the configured GeniAI layer rather than duplicating provider configuration.
What this plugin does

GeniAI Course Builder is an orchestration plugin: it receives the teacher's intent and source material, extracts usable content, asks installed activity subplugins what they can build, and presents those possibilities for selection.

The important architectural choice is that Quiz, Lesson, Assignment, Forum, Page and H5P-specific rules live in their own builders. The parent coordinates the workflow instead of becoming one giant switch statement that knows every activity Moodle may ever support.

Features you get
Multiple uploads
Use several files in the same course-building request.
Per-file intent
Describe what each file should become or how it should be used.
Pluggable activity builders
Install new generators without rewriting the parent workflow.
H5P specialization
Use dedicated builders for concrete H5P content types instead of a single generic H5P path.
Teacher review
Choose which proposed activities should actually be created.
Moodle-native result
The generated course remains editable with Moodle's own activity interfaces.

name: Plain Language
description: Review teacher-authored Moodle content for clarity using local heuristics plus constrained AI suggestions that preserve HTML and Moodle placeholders.
description_html:
Clearer course contentMoodle 4.5+

Plain Language

Find sentences, instructions and content structures that may be difficult to follow, then request semantic review or a protected rewrite without handing your HTML structure to the model to redesign.

Supported scope
Teacher-authored course text
Design focus
Preserve markup and meaning
Built as a Moodle plugin first: permissions, native APIs and human review remain part of the workflow instead of being replaced by an external black box.
Practical results
Production-minded
✓
Local heuristics first
Measures sentence length, large paragraphs, heading structure, vague link text and other objective signals without AI.
✓
Semantic review
Uses AI for ambiguity, incomplete instructions, confusing sequence, undefined terms and similar language problems.
✓
Protected rewriting
Temporarily replaces HTML and Moodle placeholders with immutable tokens before asking for a rewrite.
No automatic publishing
Suggestions are review material rather than silent edits to course content.
Markup protection
A rewrite is rejected if protected tags or placeholders are missing, duplicated or reordered.
Session-scoped cache
Repeated analysis can be reused during the current session without creating a cross-user result store.
What this plugin does

Plain Language separates mechanical readability signals from semantic judgement. PHP can count words, detect long sentences and find weak structural signals reliably; AI is reserved for cases where meaning and context matter.

Rewrite suggestions are intentionally defensive. HTML tags, links, PLUGINFILE references and Moodle/template placeholders are protected before the request, and the returned text is accepted only if those tokens come back exactly as expected.

Features you get
Content extraction
Review supported teacher-authored Moodle content without analysing learner submissions.
Deterministic metrics
Expose concrete local signals before any semantic model opinion.
Strict semantic categories
Accept only known finding categories and bounded structured output.
Safe rewrite preview
Show a suggested rewrite while preserving the original markup contract.
Bridge error handling
Keep local findings even when semantic review is unavailable.
No provider settings
Course text reviews do not require provider settings within this plugin.

Also requires AI Bridge.

name: Role Explainer
description: Explain why Moodle granted or denied a capability by reconstructing the role and context evidence while treating has_capability() as authoritative.
description_html:
Permission diagnosticsMoodle 4.5+

Role Explainer

Stop guessing why a user can or cannot do something: inspect the actual context path, role assignments, overrides and prohibitions that Moodle used.

Supported scope
Roles, contexts and capabilities
Design focus
Explain, never modify
Built as a Moodle plugin first: permissions, native APIs and human review remain part of the workflow instead of being replaced by an external black box.
Practical results
Production-minded
✓
Deterministic permission trace
Builds the evidence tree from assignments, context hierarchy and stored role capability rules.
✓
Official result wins
Moodle's own has_capability() result remains authoritative even when the reconstructed trace is displayed.
✓
Readable AI explanation
AI can translate the already-computed evidence into human language without being allowed to decide the permission.
No role writes
The plugin never changes assignments, role definitions or overrides.
Identity minimisation
The AI payload identifies the subject generically and excludes name, username, email and Moodle user ID.
Native admin links
Where permitted, the result links to Moodle's own review, assign and override screens.
What this plugin does

Role Explainer is aimed at one of Moodle administration's classic questions: why did this capability resolve this way here? It follows the real context path and shows explicit assignments, inherited rules, ALLOW, PREVENT, PROHIBIT and multi-role aggregation.

AI is optional presentation assistance. The model receives the deterministic evidence and the official result, and the prompt explicitly prevents it from inventing assignments or recalculating access.

Features you get
Context-path analysis
Inspect system, category, course, module, block and other relevant ancestor contexts.
Role aggregation
Show how multiple roles combine and where an absolute PROHIBIT changes the result.
Override visibility
Surface the closest effective capability rule for each applicable role.
Admin behavior
Account for site-administrator behavior and relevant accesslib gates.
AI-free fallback
Keep the complete deterministic diagnosis available without AI.
Actionable navigation
Open the native permissions screens when the operator has the corresponding capability.

name: Course Start Notifications
description: Notify active enrolled users when a Moodle course reaches its configured start date, with duplicate protection and retry handling.
description_html:
Automated course messagingMoodle 4.1+

Course Start Notifications

Send the course-start message when the configured start date actually arrives, using Moodle's Message API and a persistent delivery record so cron does not spam users.

Supported scope
Active course enrolments
Design focus
Reliable one-time delivery
Built as a Moodle plugin first: permissions, native APIs and human review remain part of the workflow instead of being replaced by an external black box.
Practical results
Production-minded
✓
Scheduled delivery
A task checks for newly started courses every five minutes by default.
✓
Duplicate protection
Successful delivery is recorded by course, user and start date.
✓
Start-date aware
If a course is rescheduled to a new future start date, that new occurrence can generate a new notification.
Moodle Message API
Uses Moodle's normal notification infrastructure instead of maintaining a parallel mail system.
Hidden-course control
Hidden courses are ignored by default and can be enabled explicitly in settings.
Retry window
Failed sends can be retried while the course remains inside the configured look-back period.
What this plugin does

Course Start Notifications solves a small operational problem that becomes annoying at scale: a course start date exists in Moodle, but enrolled users do not automatically receive a purpose-built start notification from that date.

The plugin watches only relevant course starts, skips historical courses from before installation, targets active enrolments and records each successful send so repeated cron executions remain idempotent.

Features you get
Translated defaults
Use the recipient's language for the default subject and message.
Custom placeholders
Insert firstname, course name, start date and course URL in custom messages.
Email delivery
Force email for this notification provider while keeping popup enabled by default.
Configurable hidden courses
Choose whether hidden courses should participate.
Manual task testing
Execute the scheduled task directly from Moodle CLI when validating setup.
No duplicate spam
Use persistent delivery state rather than relying on cron timing alone.

name: Question Audit
description: Audit existing question-bank questions with conservative local checks plus evidence-bound AI review, without generating or changing questions automatically.
description_html:
Question-bank quality reviewMoodle 4.5+

Question Audit

Review one question, selected questions or an entire category and keep objective structural checks separate from semantic review.

Supported scope
Common Moodle question types
Design focus
Audit, not generation
Built as a Moodle plugin first: permissions, native APIs and human review remain part of the workflow instead of being replaced by an external black box.
Practical results
Production-minded
✓
Question-bank actions
Adds per-question, bulk and category audit entry points to the native question bank.
✓
Deterministic checks first
Finds empty statements, duplicate answers, suspicious fractions, missing feedback and structural problems locally.
✓
Evidence-bound AI findings
Semantic findings must cite text that actually exists in the normalized question content.
No student attempts
Question attempts, learner answers and grades are not sent to AI.
No automatic changes
Suggestions remain review hypotheses and never rewrite a question by themselves.
Strict parser
Malformed JSON, unknown fields and invented evidence are rejected rather than displayed as trusted findings.
What this plugin does

Question Audit helps teachers review existing question quality instead of generating more questions. Supported types include multiple choice, true/false, short answer, numerical, essay and representable matching questions.

AI focuses on ambiguity, defensible alternative answers, wording clues, distractor quality, cognitive level, missing context and possible factual obsolescence, while PHP retains responsibility for structural facts.

Features you get
Single-question audit
Open an audit directly from an accessible question.
Bulk review
Audit selected questions without leaving the question-bank workflow.
Category audit
Review the current category while respecting question capabilities and latest versions.
Confidence visible
Keep model confidence and evidence attached to each semantic finding.
Unsupported-type handling
Report locally when a question type is not suitable for semantic auditing.
Bridge isolation
Keep provider credentials and routing outside the qbank plugin.

name: Gradebook Doctor
description: Diagnose and explain Moodle gradebook results with deterministic gradebook evidence first and AI only for read-only explanations.
description_html:
Gradebook diagnosticsMoodle 4.5+

Gradebook Doctor

Explain grades, diagnose unusual gradebook configurations and compare two students while keeping Moodle's own grade calculations authoritative.

The plugin builds a deterministic view from Moodle gradebook records and core grade classes, including aggregation status, effective weights, exclusions, overrides, locks, formulas and update state.

AI receives only a reduced representation of those facts and is used to explain the result. It does not recalculate grades, replace Moodle's final value or modify gradebook data.

Main tools
Explain this grade
Trace a grade item, category total or course total through Moodle's recorded gradebook state.
Diagnose gradebook
Flag configurations that deserve review without treating unusual settings as automatically wrong.
Compare two students
Show factual differences in values, aggregation status, exclusions, overrides, locks and weighting.
Read-only by design
Does not change grades, formulas, aggregation settings, exclusions, overrides or locks.
Core access model
Requires Gradebook Doctor access together with Moodle grader-report and grade-view capabilities.
No prompt persistence
The plugin stores no personal data, prompts or AI responses of its own.
Practical use and interpretation

Gradebook Doctor supports Moodle administrators and course teams investigating gradebook anomalies instead of correcting values blindly. The useful workflow begins with detecting inconsistencies, relating them to categories, items or calculations and identifying which configuration produced the surprising outcome. Administrators should verify findings against real grading policies before changing a gradebook, particularly in courses with overridden or locked grades. A diagnostic report helps explain the situation but should not become an automatic grade-rewriting tool.

name: AI Bridge
description: Tenant-aware AI orchestration for Moodle with purposes, logical roles, credits, route priorities, provider subplugins and usage accounting.
description_html:
AI infrastructureMoodle 4.5+

AI Bridge

Give Moodle plugins one stable AI API while centralizing provider credentials, tenant isolation, routing, quotas, credits and usage accounting.

Consumers call a provider-neutral API with a purpose and message list; the bridge resolves tenant, logical role, route priority and provider/model fallback without forcing every plugin to become its own miniature AI SDK.

Production-oriented boundaries
  • Provider integrations live in aibridge_* subplugins.
  • Provider configuration is encrypted with Moodle core encryption.
  • Custom endpoints require explicit allowlisting.
  • The parent bridge records usage metadata without persisting prompt or generated text.
Moodle para Desenvolvedores — Capítulo 32
Inteligência Artificial no Desenvolvimento Moodle

O capítulo usa a arquitetura do AI Bridge para discutir integração de IA em plugins Moodle, separação entre infraestrutura e funcionalidade, provedores, roteamento e quando vale usar as APIs de IA do core ou uma camada própria.

Ler o capítulo 32
Tenant-aware routing
Resolve tenant, purpose and logical AI role into an ordered route, allowing different institutions and user roles to use different provider/model policies.
Prioritized fallback
Routes can try providers and models in order, keeping fallback logic in one infrastructure layer instead of duplicating it across consumers.
Credits and cost accounting
Institutional credits can be managed independently from provider billing while tokens, latency, status and estimated monetary cost remain available for operational analysis.
One bridge, many Moodle features

Plugins can define purposes for their own workflows while provider selection remains centralized. This means a helpdesk assistant, course auditor, tutor or content tool can share governance and credentials without sharing business logic.

name: Personal XP
description: Add non-competitive, per-course XP and levels that emphasize each learner's own progress without leaderboards or public ranking.
description_html:
Progress without rankingMoodle 4.5+

Personal XP

Use experience points to make participation and progress visible while deliberately avoiding the leaderboard mechanics that turn progress into social status.

Supported scope
Completion, quiz, forum and course events
Design focus
Personal progression
Built as a Moodle plugin first: permissions, native APIs and human review remain part of the workflow instead of being replaced by an external black box.
Practical results
Production-minded
✓
Event-based XP
Award XP for configured Moodle learning events with duplicate protection.
✓
Private progression
Learners see their own level, next-level progress and XP history rather than a public ranking.
✓
Teacher follow-up
Teachers can inspect participants for pedagogical follow-up without sorting the report into a competition.
Idempotent awards
A stable source hash prevents the same event from accidentally granting XP twice.
Forum farming protection
A configurable daily cap limits repetitive forum-post XP.
Grades stay separate
XP can represent effort or participation without pretending to be an academic grade.
What this plugin does

Personal XP uses gamification as a progress signal rather than a race. There is no podium, league or learner-to-learner ranking: the learner competes only with their own previous progress.

The plugin stores an immutable award history plus aggregated per-course totals. Newer versions can optionally refine activity effort using AI, but PHP owns the XP formula and clamps the final award to configured limits.

Features you get
Configurable rules
Set XP for activity completion, quiz submission, forum participation and course completion.
Custom levels
Define thresholds and level names with a simple XP-to-name configuration.
Learner dashboard
Show current level, next milestone and recent XP sources.
Teacher report
Provide course-level visibility without ranking by XP.
Adaptive effort estimate
Optionally refine activity difficulty and effort using AI while keeping the formula deterministic.
Privacy API
Export and delete learner XP data through Moodle's privacy framework.

Also requires AI Bridge.

name: Duplicate Questions
description: Find exact, near-textual and semantic duplicate questions using local candidate reduction before any AI comparison.
description_html:
Duplicate detection at scaleMoodle 4.5+

Duplicate Questions

Detect likely duplicate questions without sending every possible pair to AI and without deleting anything from the question bank automatically.

Supported scope
Latest visible question versions
Design focus
Avoid N x N AI comparisons
Built as a Moodle plugin first: permissions, native APIs and human review remain part of the workflow instead of being replaced by an external black box.
Practical results
Production-minded
✓
Cheap local indexes
Normalize text, hash content, compare answer signatures and use keywords plus MinHash/LSH to build candidate buckets.
✓
Bounded AI comparison
Only pairs that survive local filters reach semantic comparison, with per-question and per-scan limits.
✓
Human decision
Teachers can inspect pairs, mark them as not duplicate or ignore them; no question is deleted automatically.
Cache invalidation
Question lifecycle changes invalidate comparisons when source hashes change.
Persistent ignore
An explicitly ignored pair stays suppressed even if its questions later change.
No learner data
Student attempts, answers, grades and enrolment information are outside the AI payload.
