name: Case AI
description: Run adaptive case-study simulations where AI writes the narrative while deterministic Moodle state controls facts, variables, rounds and completion.
description_html:
Case AI

Run adaptive case-study simulations where learners make professional decisions and AI writes the evolving narrative while authoritative facts and state remain controlled by the activity.

AI handles the narrative, not the truth

The teacher defines the scenario, learning objectives, case facts, immutable structural facts and the variables that represent the case state. Those variables can have types, initial values and allowed ranges, giving the simulation explicit boundaries before the learner begins.

Decision-by-decision simulation

During each round, the learner makes a professional decision and the AI proposes the next narrative turn together with possible state changes. The activity validates those proposed changes against the teacher-defined schema before accepting them, rejecting unknown variables, changes to immutable facts, invalid types and out-of-range values.

State stays deterministic

The persisted case state is kept separately from generated narrative text. Attempt locking, state-version checks and unique round constraints protect the workflow from replay and double submission, so a conversational response cannot silently become the authoritative source of the case state.

Teacher review remains authoritative

Teachers can review the learner's complete decision path and enter grades manually. AI may assist with narrative and summaries, but it does not own the grade and cannot bypass the deterministic rules that govern the case.

Practical use and interpretation

Case AI supports an adaptive case-study narrative while keeping authoritative scenario variables and progression rules under Moodle control. This separation matters when learners make different choices: generated narrative can vary, but the exercise still needs stable rules for state, rounds and completion. Teachers should write objectives and verify expected transitions rather than assuming the model will maintain consistency on its own. The output is a teaching simulation requiring review, not an independent source of factual decisions.

name: Personal Progress
description: Give each learner a private dashboard of XP, streaks, goals, quests, milestones, rewards and course completion without rankings.
description_html:
Personal Progress

Bring the learner's own XP, streaks, goals, quests, milestones, rewards and course completion into one compact dashboard without leaderboards or class comparisons.

One view of personal progress

The block can show the learner's current Personal XP level and total, progress toward the next level, XP earned during the current and previous week, and an eight-week personal evolution view.

When companion plugins are installed, additional cards can show the current study streak and personal best, active and completed goals, quests in progress, earned milestones, available reward credits and overall course completion.

A dashboard, not another progress engine

Personal Progress is a presentation and aggregation layer. It does not award XP, change reward balances, complete goals or write progress back into the plugins that own those records. Each source remains responsible for its own state.

Configurable cards

Each card can be enabled, disabled and positioned in the block configuration. Cards backed by optional plugins disappear cleanly when the corresponding integration is unavailable, so the dashboard can be used with only the progress sources an institution actually needs.

Progress without competition

The learner is compared only with their own previous progress. There are no positions, percentiles, class averages or messages saying that one learner is ahead of another.

Practical use and interpretation

Personal Progress gives learners a private view of their progress signals, such as goals, streaks, milestones and completed activities, without ranking classmates against one another. This approach can support self-regulation when the indicators are explained and linked to real course tasks. Teachers and administrators should avoid overemphasizing point totals where the educational objective is deeper learning. The block is most useful when a learner can identify an achievable next step and understand how recent actions changed the dashboard.

name: Personal Study Streak
description: Track each learner's own study consistency with timezone-aware streaks, milestones and optional rewards, without leaderboards.
description_html:
Personal Study Streak

Track each learner's own study consistency from meaningful course activity, with timezone-aware streaks, personal milestones and no leaderboard.

Study actions, not simple logins

The block listens to learning events such as course access, activity completion, assignment submission, quiz attempts, forum posts and resource views, then consolidates qualifying actions into one daily record per learner and course. A Moodle login by itself does not count as a study day.

Multiple qualifying actions on the same date increase the day's activity count without artificially extending the streak more than once.

Streaks that respect the learner's calendar

Day boundaries are calculated in the learner's configured timezone. Teachers can configure ignored weekdays, so a schedule that excludes weekends can carry a Friday streak into Monday without pretending Saturday and Sunday were active study days.

Protected missed days can preserve an existing streak without being counted as active days.

Personal milestones

The learner can follow the current streak, personal best, active days and upcoming milestones. Configured milestones can also connect to optional rewards such as XP, credits or badges when the corresponding integrations are available.

Consistency without competition

The block is intentionally personal: it does not rank learners, compare streaks or expose another learner's consistency. The objective is to make study continuity visible without converting routine learning activity into a class competition.

name: Personal Goals
description: Let learners create and follow private course goals with extensible goal types, progress tracking and optional XP and reward integrations.
description_html:
Personal Goals

Give each learner a private space to define study goals, follow progress toward their own targets and build self-regulation without rankings or comparisons with classmates.

Goals based on real learning activity

Learners can create goals around XP gained after the goal starts, active study days, completed activities, overall course completion, submitted quiz attempts, selected activities or accumulated study time. The available target therefore depends on measurable learning progress rather than a generic checklist.

Flexible time periods

A goal can apply to the current day, week or month, use a custom date range or have no deadline. Calendar boundaries follow the learner's configured timezone, avoiding the common problem where progress near midnight is counted on the wrong day.

Private progress and history

Learners see their current progress against the target, while goals move through active, completed, expired and cancelled states. Completed goals become part of the learner's own history, and an older goal can be used as the basis for creating a new one.

Optional progress integrations

When companion plugins are available, Personal Goals can use their public APIs for information such as Personal XP and can connect goal completion to celebration or reward experiences. These integrations remain optional and do not turn the feature into a competitive leaderboard.

name: Reward Shop
description: Provide a course reward store with spendable credits kept separate from XP, immutable ledger history and safe idempotent purchases.
description_html:
Reward Shop

Add a non-competitive reward store where learners spend course credits while their historical XP remains untouched.

Credits and XP serve different purposes

Reward Shop keeps spendable credits separate from Personal XP. XP represents accumulated learning progress and is never consumed by a purchase, while the course wallet contains the balance that can actually be spent on rewards.

Each wallet keeps the current balance together with totals earned and spent, while every movement is recorded in an immutable ledger. Corrections are represented as new refunds or adjustments instead of rewriting older transactions.

Different kinds of rewards
  • Existing Moodle badges.
  • Content entitlements.
  • Hints.
  • Teacher-approved custom requests.
Purchases designed to resist duplicates

Reward prices are taken from the server rather than trusted from the browser. Wallet updates use locking and database transactions, and each purchase carries an idempotency token so double clicks, reloads or repeated requests do not intentionally charge the same purchase twice.

Optional Personal XP conversion

Courses can define rules that grant credits when cumulative XP milestones are reached. The conversion is idempotent, so synchronizing progress repeatedly does not grant the same milestone credit again, and XP itself remains unchanged after the conversion.

Practical use and interpretation

Reward Shop organizes the exchange of earned learning credits or rewards through a controlled course workflow. Institutions can connect incentives to defined progression rules while keeping redemption records visible to authorized staff. The important operational questions are which balances can be spent, what the reward grants, when it is available and how a mistaken redemption should be reviewed. Rewards should reinforce meaningful activity instead of turning an educational program into a competition for arbitrary points.

name: XP Celebration
description: Queue accessible personal celebrations for level-ups, XP milestones, goals, quests, rewards and course progress without competitive comparison.
description_html:
XP Celebration

Give learners positive visual feedback when meaningful personal milestones are reached, without rankings or comparisons with other learners.

Celebrate progress that already happened

The plugin does not calculate XP itself. Instead, it reacts to progress recorded by other parts of the learning experience and queues celebrations for events such as level changes, cumulative XP milestones and important course-progress moments.

Companion plugins can also request celebrations for completed goals, streaks, quests, unlocked rewards, personal records and other supported milestone types.

A persisted celebration queue

Celebrations are stored before they are shown and are claimed one at a time when the learner returns to a related course page. This prevents a simple reload from replaying the same celebration repeatedly or silently consuming several milestones at once.

Different presentation styles
  • Modal presentation for prominent milestones.
  • Toast-style feedback for lighter events.
  • Achievement-style presentation for accomplishments.
  • Configurable visual themes and animation choices.
Designed for personal motivation

The experience respects reduced-motion preferences and keeps sound disabled by default. The focus stays on acknowledging the learner's own progress rather than turning every achievement into a comparison with the rest of the class.

Practical use and interpretation

XP Celebration provides lightweight recognition of learner milestones and achievements within an existing progress system. A brief celebration can make progress visible without creating another grading mechanism or public ranking. Administrators should keep the presentation proportionate to the achievement and accessible to users who prefer reduced visual motion. The value lies in giving timely, understandable feedback about a defined milestone rather than encouraging constant notifications for insignificant actions.

name: XP Quests
description: Build personal learning quests from Moodle actions with deterministic progression, repeatable runs and optional XP and credit rewards.
description_html:
XP Quests

Build personal learning quests from real course actions, with sequential or any-order progression, repeatable runs and optional XP, credit and celebration rewards.

Compose quests from learning actions

Teachers can create quests using steps such as viewing or completing an activity, submitting a quiz attempt, passing a quiz, posting in a forum, submitting an assignment, completing a course section, reaching an XP target or receiving manual confirmation.

Quests can require steps in sequence or allow them in any order, can use availability dates and may be configured for repeated execution.

Each learner follows their own quest

Progress is private to the learner and each repeatable execution is stored separately. There is no leaderboard or class ranking, so quests are used to structure personal progression rather than to compare participants.

Completion comes from trusted course state

Automatic steps are completed by Moodle events or server-side state checks rather than by accepting a learner-supplied claim that the step is finished. Manual steps require an authorized confirmation.

Rewards without duplicate delivery

Quest completion can award XP through Personal XP and can optionally connect to Reward Shop credits and XP Celebration feedback. Separate completion and reward records make repeated events, reloads and retries safe against intentionally granting the same reward twice.

Practical use and interpretation

XP Quests combines defined course actions into personal learning quests with deterministic progression and optional rewards. Teachers can create a sequence of goals that encourages continued engagement without relying on leaderboards. Clear completion criteria matter: participants should know which action advances a quest and how repeatable quests are handled. Administrators should keep reward calculations auditable and guard against duplicate credit grants when the same event is processed again.

name: OabFlix
description: OAB-focused streaming-style Moodle child theme built on EadFlix, with featured content, continue watching, curated course rows, Areas of Law and live editorial content.
description_html:
OabFlix

Give OAB preparation courses a streaming-inspired front page while continuing to use native courses, categories, enrolments and completion data.

A front page built around course discovery

OabFlix presents a large featured area that can be configured manually or connected to a course. When a course is used, its title, summary, image and link become the featured content, keeping the presentation tied to material that already exists in the learning environment.

The theme also provides a continue-watching row based on the current learner's enrolments, last access and course-completion progress, helping learners return to courses they have already started.

Curated OAB content
  • Ordered highlights selected by configured course IDs.
  • OAB preparation section populated from a configured course category.
  • Areas of Law built from visible child categories under a configured root category.
  • Native course search for finding additional content.
  • Configurable OabFlix Live block with title, text, image and destination link.
Editorial choices without fake popularity

If no explicit highlight list is configured, the theme can fall back to recently modified visible courses and presents them as catalogue highlights rather than pretending that technical ordering represents audience popularity.

Focused customization on top of EadFlix

OabFlix is implemented as a child theme of EadFlix, so the OAB-specific work stays concentrated on the front-page experience while the broader course interface, accessibility tooling, login, profile, footer and activity presentation continue to come from the parent theme.

name: Video Bridge
description: Provide a shared video source and player layer for Moodle activities with reusable providers, capability discovery and consistent runtime adapters. Requires AI Bridge.
description_html:
Video infrastructureMoodle 4.5+

Video Bridge

Give Moodle video activities one shared source and player layer while keeping progress, grading, completion, quizzes, annotations and other activity rules inside each consumer plugin.

Supported sources
Upload, URL, YouTube, Vimeo, Nextcloud, Google Drive, Panda Video, OTTFlix and iframe
Design focus
Reusable providers without duplicating player code across activities
Video Bridge contains source infrastructure only. Consumer activities remain responsible for their own pedagogical behavior and Moodle completion or grading rules.
Practical results
Shared runtime
✓
One provider manager
Activities discover sources, add form fields, normalize records and obtain player configuration through one API.
✓
Capability-aware sources
Providers declare tracking, seeking, playback control and playback-rate support so consumers know what can safely be required.
✓
Consistent adapters
AMD adapters expose the same play, pause, time, duration, rate, seek and normalized event surface.
Protected Moodle upload
Use Moodle-managed files as a native protected source without forcing each activity to implement its own upload layer.
Provider-specific capability flags
Iframe-based sources can remain valid for playback even when reliable tracking or player control is unavailable.
Shared runtime libraries
HLS and Vimeo runtime dependencies are shipped by Video Bridge so consumer plugins do not depend on mod_videoprogress assets.
What this plugin does

Video Bridge centralizes the technical problem every Moodle video activity otherwise ends up solving again: where the video comes from, which player adapter should be used and which controls the provider can actually support.

Activities remain intentionally decoupled from that infrastructure. A progress activity may require tracking, a branching activity may require seeking and playback control, while a simple viewing activity may accept a provider that only supports playback.

Features you get
Multiple video sources
Protected uploads, direct HTML5/HLS URLs, YouTube, Vimeo, public Nextcloud shares, Google Drive preview, Panda Video, OTTFlix and cooperative iframe embeds.
Reusable form integration
Add source selectors and provider configuration fields to consumer activity forms through the shared manager.
Normalized player configuration
Convert each provider's stored settings into a stable runtime configuration consumed by the activity.
Capability discovery
Filter available providers by requirements such as tracking, seeking, playback control or playback-rate support.
Stable adapter API
Keep consumer JavaScript independent from the different APIs exposed by HTML5, YouTube, Vimeo and embedded providers.
Backward-compatible source prefix
Historical videoprogresssource_* provider components remain usable so existing configurations and backups do not become a second plugin family.
Activities using Video Bridge

The following Moodle activities use this shared infrastructure for video sources, playback progress, timeline interactions or analytics. They are separate plugins and are not bundled with Video Bridge.

  • Video Progress (mod_videoprogress)
  • Video Summary (mod_videosummary)
  • Video Reactions (mod_videoreactions)
  • Video Tracker Pro (mod_videotrackerpro)
  • Video Tracker Max (mod_videotrackermax)
  • Video Tracker Prime (mod_videotrackerprime)
  • Video Tracker Ultra (mod_videotrackerultra)
  • Video Tracker Ultimate (mod_videotrackerultimate)
  • Video Tracker Premium (mod_videotrackerpremium)

Each activity specifies its own minimum compatible Video Bridge version in its README.

Also requires AI Bridge.

name: Video Forum
description: Create asynchronous video discussions where teachers and learners publish short videos and reply with video in a Reels-style experience.
description_html:
Video Forum

Run asynchronous discussions through short video posts and video replies instead of adapting the traditional text forum.

Learners can record directly in the browser or upload supported video files, while teachers control topic creation, replies, deadlines, groups and participation requirements.

Video-first discussion threads

Video Forum is a standalone activity for asynchronous discussion through short video posts and replies, using a vertically browsable feed rather than a text-first forum with occasional attachments. Participants discuss a topic in their own words and can respond to other videos with new recordings.

  • Record with a camera and microphone in the browser, review, and then publish.
  • Upload an existing video when permitted by the activity settings.
  • Reply to a topic or another reply while preserving thread context.
  • Configure publication deadlines, duration limits and reply permissions.
  • Apply group visibility, moderation, participation grading and completion rules.
Practical workflow

Teachers define the participation rules and open the activity. Learners create a short video topic, browse permitted discussions and publish video replies. Playback of one post pauses when another starts, keeping the feed manageable. Teachers can moderate posts and review contributions without converting the discussion back into a conventional text forum.

The activity has its own publication and permission model; it does not simply reskin Moodle's standard Forum module.

name: Video Reactions
description: Let learners attach reactions to exact moments in a video timeline and explore individual or class-level reaction patterns. Requires Video Bridge.
description_html:
Also requires Video Bridge.

Video Reactions

Attach lightweight learner reactions to exact timestamps in a video.

Reactions can be grouped around nearby moments, viewed individually or across the class and displayed during playback without turning the activity into a quiz.

Reactions tied to video moments

Video Reactions collects lightweight responses at specific timestamps rather than leaving learners to react to an entire video as a single object. Its purpose is to make interesting, confusing or notable moments visible to participants and teachers.

  • Attach reactions to the exact playback position.
  • Aggregate nearby reactions into readable timeline markers.
  • Choose which reactions learners can send.
  • Control reaction frequency with teacher-configured anti-spam limits.
  • Inspect individual and group-level reaction patterns in reports.
Practical workflow

Teachers select the available reaction options and configure participation settings. While watching, a learner marks a moment with a quick reaction. The activity records the timestamp, can show concentrated reactions along the timeline and gives the teacher a view of which segments attracted responses. Optional completion and participation grading can be configured.

A reaction is an expression or feedback signal, not a graded answer or evidence that the viewer understood the material.

Practical use and interpretation

Reaction peaks can be used to plan discussion: a teacher may revisit a timestamp where learners frequently marked uncertainty or enthusiasm and ask what made that segment distinctive. The result remains subjective feedback rather than a measurement of learning. Clear anti-spam settings also matter so one participant cannot overwhelm the class timeline with repeated clicks. A small selection of meaningful reactions often works better than dozens of ambiguous symbols.

name: Video Rubric
description: Collect learner video submissions and grade them with a rubric permanently visible beside the player, including timestamped and audio feedback.
description_html:
Video Rubric

Evaluate learner video submissions without leaving the playback screen.

The grading workspace keeps the player and timeline on one side and the rubric, scores and feedback on the other, with AJAX saving and support for timestamped and audio feedback.

Grade videos with the rubric beside the player

Video Rubric combines video submissions with criterion-based assessment, keeping the media and the grading form visible together. It is especially helpful for practical demonstrations, presentations and performances where feedback must refer to a precise instant in a recording.

  • Accept supported uploaded files or browser-camera recordings.
  • Keep recordings as editable drafts until students explicitly submit.
  • Display a persistent rubric alongside the video.
  • Add timestamped comments, written observations and supported audio feedback.
  • Finalize grades through Moodle Gradebook and configure completion.
Practical workflow

A student records or uploads an attempt, previews it and submits the final version. The teacher opens the grading queue, watches the video while selecting rubric levels and annotating relevant timestamps, then finalizes the evaluation. Submission status distinguishes drafts, submitted work, ongoing grading and completed evaluations.

Recordings use Moodle's File API and access checks; saving a draft does not silently expose it as a final submission.

Practical use and interpretation

For performance assessment, timestamped feedback makes the grading explanation much easier to verify: a rubric level can be discussed alongside the exact move, phrase or demonstration that informed it. Draft and final submission states also matter operationally, because students need to know when the recording can still be replaced. Teachers should test recording and upload formats on the target devices and explain whether audio feedback is available for the configured activity.

name: Screen Recorder
description: Add browser-based screen recording to Moodle TinyMCE with configurable duration, webcam and microphone permissions and Moodle File API storage.
description_html:
Screen Recorder

Record the screen directly from TinyMCE and insert the resulting video into Moodle content.

Administrators can control recording duration and whether webcam or microphone capture is allowed, while uploaded recordings use Moodle capabilities, context checks and the File API.

Record and embed demonstrations from TinyMCE

Screen Recorder adds a browser capture workflow directly to the Moodle TinyMCE toolbar. It helps authors show how to perform a task, present a slide deck or explain what is happening on screen without leaving their text editor to prepare a separate upload.

  • Choose a screen, application window or browser tab using built-in sharing controls.
  • Optionally capture microphone and supported shared audio.
  • Include the webcam as picture-in-picture when enabled and supported.
  • Review the result before inserting it into the editor.
  • Save the recorded media through Moodle's normal editor draft-file lifecycle.
Practical workflow

The author clicks the recorder button, grants the desired permissions, records a demonstration and previews the finished video. When inserted, the media is attached to the editor's existing draft area and follows the surrounding form when it is saved. Recording stops if browser screen sharing ends.

Camera, microphone and screen permissions remain explicit. Available capture options depend on the browser, platform and administrator settings.

Practical use and interpretation

The editor integration matters for ordinary course authoring: a short software demonstration can be captured, reviewed and inserted in the same writing task instead of passing through a separate hosting service. Administrators can control whether webcam, microphone and presentation options are available to particular roles. Authors should check audio levels and the visibility of sensitive windows before recording, because the resulting video becomes part of the published Moodle content.

name: Video Tracker Pro
description: Inspect detailed video playback analytics per learner and session, including watched segments, pauses, seeks, rates, abandonment and completion. Requires Video Bridge.
description_html:
Also requires Video Bridge.

Video Tracker Pro

Understand exactly how each learner consumed a video across one or more playback sessions.

Reports expose effective watch time, viewed and repeated segments, pauses, seeks, playback speed, abandonment points, session duration and whether the learner reached the end.

Session-level viewing evidence

Video Tracker Pro helps a teacher understand the playback history behind a learner's watched percentage. Instead of a single progress bar, it separates sessions, effective playback, pauses, seeking and repeated regions into detailed evidence.

  • Inspect chronological playback sessions for individual learners.
  • Compare unique watched coverage with repeated or skipped segments.
  • Review pauses, seeks, observed playback rates and playback time.
  • See where playback last stopped and whether a session reached the end.
  • Use detailed reports within Moodle's reporting permissions and group rules.
Practical workflow

An authorized teacher opens a learner report, examines the individual session records and relates them to the sections of video the learner actually viewed. Multiple short sessions may reflect normal study patterns, while a replay peak can indicate deliberate review. Metrics are presented so that the interpretation remains with the teacher.

These measurements describe player activity. They cannot establish motivation, attention or actual learning on their own.

Practical use and interpretation

When reviewing learner evidence, compare watched coverage with effective playback and repeated sections before drawing conclusions from total session time. A short session that ended early may be an interruption, a deliberate study break or a technical problem. The report helps describe what the player recorded, while the teacher retains responsibility for interpreting the behavior in the course context.

name: Video Tracker Ultra
description: Validate video consumption against configurable rules such as minimum coverage, real watch time, playback speed, seeks and required segments. Requires Video Bridge.
description_html:
Also requires Video Bridge.

Video Tracker Ultra

Decide whether a learner's video consumption satisfies explicit validity rules instead of relying on a single progress percentage.

Teachers can require minimum watched coverage and real playback time, constrain seeks and playback speed and require specific timeline segments, including the beginning or end of the video.

Explainable viewing-rule validation

Video Tracker Ultra evaluates whether measurable playback evidence meets teacher-defined conditions. The focus is not just how much media was consumed, but which configured requirements were satisfied, violated or remain pending.

  • Set minimum watched percentage and effective viewing time.
  • Limit forward seeks, seek distance or playback speed.
  • Require specific segments, the beginning or the end of a video.
  • Configure session counts, continuous playback or inactivity tolerance.
  • Inspect rule-specific results, evidence and completion states.
Practical workflow

Teachers define validity rules that correspond to their instructional or compliance requirements. After playback, the activity evaluates recorded evidence on the server and reports whether the learner meets the conditions. Rules involving unavailable player measurements must not be treated as verified simply because a video was opened.

A valid status confirms only those observable conditions; it is not a measure of knowledge or understanding.

Practical use and interpretation

The strongest validity rules are those that reflect an explicit institutional requirement and can be reliably measured by the chosen source. Requiring a starting segment or limiting seeks may be appropriate in a defined compliance scenario, but should not be applied universally without explanation. Teachers should preview the rules and review any invalid status against its actual evidence rather than equating a rule violation with misconduct.

name: Video Tracker Max
description: Analyze collective video consumption through class heatmaps, retention curves and group comparisons built from shared Video Bridge telemetry. Requires Video Bridge.
description_html:
Also requires Video Bridge.

Video Tracker Max

See how the class is consuming a video rather than inspecting only isolated learner sessions.

Collective analytics include timeline heatmaps, reach percentages, retention patterns and comparisons between groups or cohorts using recorded playback data.

Collective video-consumption analytics

Video Tracker Max explains how a permitted class or cohort consumes video content as a whole. It produces collective views of watched regions, retention, repetition, pauses and drop-off so teachers can inspect patterns without opening every learner individually.

  • Timeline heatmaps of audience reach.
  • Retention curves that include the selected population denominator.
  • Replay, pause, seek and drop-off concentrations.
  • Period, group, grouping and cohort comparison options where permitted.
  • Authorized individual drill-down and consolidated CSV reporting.
Practical workflow

Teachers choose the permitted population and reporting period, then inspect which moments drew repeated viewing or where fewer learners continued. Comparing two groups may reveal different viewing patterns but does not, by itself, explain the causes of those differences. Aggregated reporting reduces repeated raw-event processing.

Collective reports follow Moodle groups and minimum-population privacy rules. A chart is descriptive evidence, not proof of learner comprehension.

Practical use and interpretation

One practical use of the heatmap is comparing how different learner groups reached a difficult explanation. If several viewers replayed a segment, the teacher may decide to clarify it in the next lesson, but the chart cannot identify the reason for the replay. Applying the same filters and population threshold to comparisons is essential to avoid making two fundamentally different groups look directly equivalent.

name: Video Tracker Prime
description: Place lightweight pedagogical checkpoints on a video timeline using messages, confirmations, short reflections and simple scale interactions. Requires Video Bridge.
description_html:
Also requires Video Bridge.

Video Tracker Prime

Turn selected timeline moments into lightweight pedagogical checkpoints without building a full video quiz.

Checkpoints can present information, request confirmation, collect a short reflection or ask for a simple scale response while keeping interactions synchronized with playback.

Small checkpoints on the video timeline

Video Tracker Prime adds short learner interactions at particular video moments without introducing the complexity of a formal quiz. Teachers can reinforce a concept, request a reflection or ask for a quick confirmation while the media is playing.

  • Messages, alerts, complementary links and passage checkpoints.
  • Short reflections, confidence scales and ungraded polls.
  • Required, dismissible or session-specific interactions.
  • A visual editor that places checkpoints at the current timestamp.
  • Reporting on completed checkpoints and responses.
Practical workflow

A teacher selects a moment in the video and creates a small interaction. During effective playback the prompt appears, optionally pauses the player and records the learner's response. Completion can combine the required checkpoints with viewing progress, while reports show which prompts were answered or remain pending.

Skipping over a marker does not count as completing its interaction. The plugin is not designed to replace a graded video quiz.

Practical use and interpretation

Good checkpoints have a clear instructional purpose: ask learners to commit to a prediction, name an observation or confirm a key instruction before continuing. Teachers should test the timeline events with the permitted video source, particularly when a checkpoint depends on pausing or preventing continuation. The report then reflects actual interactions instead of inferring them from the learner's final playback position.

name: Video Tracker Ultimate
description: Combine advanced video evidence into a configurable and explainable engagement score with weighted indicators and transparent scoring reasons. Requires Video Bridge.
description_html:
Video Tracker Ultimate

Build a transparent Engagement Score from real video playback evidence, with rules teachers configure and learners can understand.

Rather than producing a mysterious score, the activity lets teachers select measurable viewing indicators, give each a weight and explain precisely how the learner's result was calculated.

Configurable Engagement Score

Create indicators with individual weights, thresholds and optional mandatory completion requirements, including:

  • Minimum percentage of video actually watched and minimum effective viewing time.
  • Minimum or maximum number of playback sessions.
  • Maximum observed playback speed and maximum number of seeks.
  • Minimum number of replays and whether the learner reached the end.
  • Coverage of specific required segments of the video timeline.

Minimum targets and segment coverage can award proportional points, while pass/fail indicators use explicit conditions. Reports show each indicator's observed value, target, ratio, awarded points and weight. When weights do not add up to 100, both the raw result and normalized 0–100 score remain visible.

Reports with inspectable evidence

The teacher dashboard provides average scores, score distribution, completion rates, viewing time, learners below a review threshold and indicators most often not met. Individual reports expose viewing sessions, watched segments, metrics and the full scoring breakdown. CSV export and an optional teacher-only ranking are available, with Moodle group permissions respected.

Completion, grading and recalculation

Activity completion can require a minimum Engagement Score, watched percentage or selected mandatory indicators. Gradebook integration is optional and disabled by default; when enabled, the normalized score is scaled to the configured maximum grade.

Scores can be recalculated after rule changes through automated tasks or a teacher-only action, and saved results record their calculation time and origin.

Privacy and responsible interpretation

Access to reports follows Moodle capabilities and group visibility. The Privacy API supports export of the learner's metrics and scoring details, while backup and restore preserve activity rules without carrying learner analytics into another course.

An Engagement Score describes whether configured playback conditions were satisfied. It does not establish attention, understanding, ability or actual learning.

Also requires Video Bridge.

name: Super Video Tracker
description: Track a package of multiple videos inside one Moodle activity, including item-level progress and an overall consumption or compliance percentage.
description_html:
Super Video Tracker

Track several videos as one learning or compliance package rather than treating them as an ordinary playlist.

Each item can use a different video source while the activity reports individual video progress and the learner's overall package completion.

Also requires Video Bridge.

One training package, several videos

Super Video Tracker combines multiple required and optional videos into one trackable Moodle activity. Its purpose is to manage package-level progress and completion, not simply present an automatically playing playlist.

  • Configure required and optional items independently.
  • Set a minimum watched percentage for each required video.
  • Calculate simple or weighted package progress.
  • Complete the package when all required items, a target count or weighted progress meet the rule.
  • Review a learner-by-video progress matrix and export CSV.
Practical workflow

A teacher builds a package, chooses which media are mandatory and decides whether all required items or an aggregate threshold determines success. Students view the available media and see how each item contributes to completion. The teacher can identify the exact remaining items instead of inferring completion from one average.

Optional media do not lower required progress. The package is not inherently a locked sequence, and item availability windows may be configured separately.

Practical use and interpretation

A package-level report is especially useful for mandatory induction and recurring training, where 'completed' means all relevant items satisfy known rules. Teachers can identify the one required media item holding a participant back, while optional material remains available without penalizing package progress. Weighting should be explained clearly so learners understand why watching two equal-length videos may affect the overall percentage differently.

name: Video Tracker Premium
description: Manage operational video compliance with start dates, deadlines, grace periods, reminders, overdue learners and completion follow-up. Requires Video Bridge.
description_html:
Also requires Video Bridge.

Video Tracker Premium

Answer who must watch, who already watched and who needs to be reminded.

The activity combines watched progress with deadlines, grace periods, configurable reminders, overdue follow-up and operational compliance reporting.

Deadlines and follow-up for required viewing

Video Tracker Premium manages the operational side of mandatory video consumption, including who needs to watch, what deadline applies and which learners require a reminder or an authorized exception.

  • Availability dates, deadlines, grace periods and optional late viewing.
  • Reminders before and after the deadline through Moodle messaging.
  • Compliance statuses for completed, pending, due-soon and overdue learners.
  • Individual deadline extensions, waivers and auditable administration notes.
  • Bulk follow-up controls and CSV compliance exports.
Practical workflow

Course staff define the viewing threshold and deadline, then monitor participation in a status dashboard. Scheduled processing prepares appropriate reminders with duplicate protection. Authorized staff may issue an extension or waiver without changing the original deadline for everyone in the course.

An overdue status records a missed configured condition, not the reason a learner was unable to finish. Messaging depends on the site's normal Moodle message-delivery configuration.

Practical use and interpretation

Operational follow-up works best when reminders, extensions and waivers have clear ownership. An overdue learner may need an accommodation, not another automated message, so staff should be able to review the visible status and apply a documented exception where appropriate. The notification log and administrative history help explain why a person received a reminder or was marked compliant on a particular date.

name: Authorship
description: Record evidence about how textual answers were produced during proctored attempts, including typing, paste, deletion and editing behavior.
description_html:
Authorship

Capture factual evidence about how textual answers were produced during a proctored attempt.

The policy records active writing time, typed, pasted and removed characters and significant insertion or deletion events without claiming to detect whether an answer was written by AI.

How a written answer was produced

Authorship is a policy extension for Kopere Proctoring that records the editing process of textual quiz answers. It is intended to help a human reviewer understand writing behavior, not to label an answer as AI-generated or determine cheating automatically.

  • Aggregate typing, deletion, paste and replacement events.
  • Record writing duration, revisions and unusually large insertions.
  • Keep periodic snapshots and meaningful editing deltas.
  • Display a compact writing timeline for authorized review.
  • Reconstruct the evolution of an answer from available snapshots.
Practical workflow

During an enabled quiz attempt, textual input is observed and summarized in batches instead of storing every keystroke as a separate database event. Reviewers can inspect how the answer developed, including paste activity and subsequent editing, when evaluating an incident in its broader context.

Pasting or rewriting is not proof of misconduct. This policy records evidence only and leaves interpretation to responsible staff.

Practical use and interpretation

The writing timeline can help reviewers distinguish a response typed gradually from one assembled through large edits, but those patterns admit many legitimate explanations. Assistive technologies, prepared notes, copying from a permitted resource and normal drafting habits may all affect the observed sequence. Institutions should communicate what is recorded, protect sensitive response content and retain a human process for interpreting an alert.

name: Mastery Practice
description: Create adaptive practice sessions from Moodle Question Bank content, prioritizing weak or fading knowledge through mastery and spaced repetition.
description_html:
Mastery Practice

Use Moodle Question Bank content for adaptive practice focused on what each learner currently knows and what is beginning to fade.

The activity reuses Moodle questions, categories, tags and the Question Engine while prioritizing weaker topics and spaced review instead of randomly drawing every topic equally.

Adaptive Question Bank practice and review

Mastery Practice uses Moodle's native Question Bank and Question Engine to offer sessions shaped by each learner's previous practice. Rather than sampling all questions uniformly, it prioritizes concepts that are due for review or have weak mastery evidence.

  • Build short practice sessions from question categories and tags.
  • Prioritize overdue reviews, low mastery and configured critical concepts.
  • Offer Leitner, SM-2 and adaptive mastery scheduling strategies.
  • Show concept progress including in-progress, mastered and review-overdue states.
  • Provide teacher views of concept gaps and configurable completion criteria.
Practical workflow

Teachers configure the source questions, the concept model and the practice schedule. A learner answers a targeted set of questions and receives another review opportunity according to the selected strategy. The activity manages when questions return, while Moodle itself renders and evaluates the questions.

An estimated mastery state helps schedule further practice. It is not a replacement for a formal assessment or a claim that one successful response proves lasting understanding.

name: Moodle MCP
description: Expose Moodle through a secure and extensible Model Context Protocol server with OAuth 2.1, PKCE, manual tokens and separated read/write APIs.
description_html:
Moodle MCP

Turn Moodle into a secure Model Context Protocol server for MCP clients, agents and future ChatGPT integrations.

The plugin provides its own OAuth 2.1 authorization model with Authorization Code and PKCE, refresh tokens, manual integration tokens, discovery endpoints and deliberately separated read and write APIs.

Secure Moodle access for MCP clients

Moodle MCP gives compatible Model Context Protocol clients a structured way to inspect and manage permitted Moodle resources. It is a server hosted by the Moodle installation, not an unrestricted database gateway, and each connected user remains subject to the normal permissions of the site.

  • OAuth 2.1 authorization, PKCE and scoped access for connected clients.
  • Separate READ and WRITE tool surfaces, plus an endpoint for clients that need both.
  • Write previews and explicit confirmations for protected changes.
  • Extensible tool discovery: other compatible Moodle plugins can contribute their own MCP tools.
  • Course, category, user and site operations limited by Moodle capabilities.
Practical workflow

An administrator enables the integration and authorizes a supported client. The client discovers available tools and can inspect resources before requesting a change. Operations that require confirmation expose a preview so the user can check what will be changed rather than trusting a free-form instruction to execute silently.

Authentication, token revocation, audit records and context validation are part of the workflow. A tool's presence does not automatically grant the connected user permission to run it.

name: Sanitized Clone
description: Experimental CLI-only sanitization and privacy inventory for isolated Moodle clones, with guarded authorization, checkpoints and deliberately incomplete coverage.
description_html:
Isolated staging clonesExperimental implementation

Sanitized Clone

Inspect and sanitize selected information inside an already isolated Moodle clone, with explicit authorization and a checkpointed CLI process instead of a dangerous one-click production operation.

Sanitized Clone provides an administrator-facing inventory, fixed sanitization stages and auditable execution for a test installation. It is deliberately conservative: the current engine cannot certify that an arbitrary production-derived Moodle copy is free of personal information or secrets.

Current capabilities
  • Preflight inventory, fixed stage profiles, authorization and execution history.
  • Deterministic HMAC-based names and unique example.invalid account addresses.
  • Selected text-field scrubbing, session and credential cleanup, and guarded File API handling.
  • CLI-only execution with database checkpoints, locking and a technical JSON manifest.
Isolated destination
The target requires separate database, dataroot, credentials and an out-of-band destination attestation. Network and integration isolation must already be enforced by infrastructure.
Controlled processing
Bounded keyset batches, transactions and checkpoints allow the operator to inspect progress and handle interruptions without treating every file or field as safe to rewrite.
Fail-closed inventory
Uncovered tables, partially reviewed schemas and unknown file areas remain blocking findings rather than being silently counted as sanitized.
What sanitization actually proves

An administrator creates a fixed-stage profile, checks the preflight inventory and authorizes a destination for a limited window. The sanitization engine runs from the destination command line using a protected attestation file, while the web interface exposes status and audit information without a destructive HTTP endpoint.

The implementation preserves numeric identifiers and Moodle relationships while transforming selected identity fields and selected free-text records. It does not globally replace content in serialized objects, arbitrary HTML, external services or third-party tables; those sources require dedicated, schema-aware handling.

Final approval remains blocked when coverage is incomplete. A successful execution or an exit code reporting unresolved sources is not a privacy certification, and administrators must independently review external storage, backups, plugins and written course content.

Experimental and not production-data approved: do not expose a cloned dataset to developers or a public test environment solely because this process ran. Complete coverage and independent isolation checks are prerequisites.

name: Site Configuration Diff
description: Compare sanitized configuration snapshots across Moodle environments and selectively apply a restricted set of safe core settings.
description_html:
Configuration comparisonOffline-first workflow

Site Configuration Diff

Export sanitized Moodle configuration snapshots, compare them across environments and inspect a controlled change plan without giving one installation remote administration access to another.

Moving settings between development, staging and production is rarely a matter of copying a configuration table. Site Configuration Diff makes changes reviewable while keeping secret values out of transferred snapshots and restricting which differences can ever be applied.

Comparison and control
  • Sanitized JSON snapshots include Moodle release and plugin/version manifests.
  • Compare two imported snapshots or an imported snapshot with the current site.
  • Inspect added, removed, modified, missing and redacted settings.
  • Create a persistent preview and require separate authorization before allowed writes.
Secrets stay redacted
Only a small reviewed list of core values is exported visibly; all other configuration entries are represented as present-but-redacted rather than exporting credentials or their hashes.
Strict write boundary
Version 1.0.x restricts automated changes to core language, country and timezone with validation; theme, calendar and plugin settings are not automatically applied.
Audit and concurrency
The operator must have the apply capability and appear on a numeric allowlist. Every selected value is rechecked against the live site before execution.
A safer path between environments

An administrator exports a bounded snapshot and transports the JSON through an approved channel. The destination imports it using schema, checksum and size checks, and presents an understandable difference report with installation and plugin context.

Read-only comparisons never alter configuration. When the target is the current site, privileged operators can select explicitly eligible settings and store a preview plan. A second approval applies only the allowed entries, and stale values are rejected rather than overwriting intervening administrator changes.

The snapshot checksum detects accidental or deliberate content changes but does not authenticate who created the file. For origin assurance, use signed transfer or another trusted out-of-band mechanism; the plugin deliberately avoids executing imported PHP or contacting another installation.

Limited application scope: comparison is wider than automatic writing. In this release only core:lang, core:country and core:timezone are eligible for approval-based updates.

name: Backup Drill
description: Test Moodle course backup restorability through real restores and structural checks in an isolated lab environment.
description_html:
Restore rehearsalDedicated test laboratory

Backup Drill

Prove more than archive readability by actually restoring Moodle course backups in a disposable, isolated test site and examining the resulting course against the backup manifest.

A backup file can unpack successfully and still fail when Moodle attempts its restore plan, resolves dependencies or reconstructs activities. Backup Drill turns that uncertainty into a repeatable operational test with recorded outcomes and controlled cleanup.

Test-lab workflow
  • Import an .mbz archive into the lab using Moodle File API or CLI.
  • Execute native prechecks and restore_controller in a temporary course.
  • Review manifest counts, missing components, warnings and run history.
  • Schedule rehearsals and inspect technical JSON/CSV reports with restricted access.
Real restore execution
The lab uses the actual Moodle restore process rather than counting ZIP entries and reporting archive integrity as a successful course restoration.
Isolated operations
Use a separate database, moodledata and credentials, deny outbound network traffic at infrastructure level and restrict disposable courses to a dedicated hidden category.
Conservative result states
Runs distinguish archive failures, restore failures, partial results and warnings. Evidence that cannot yet be verified is identified instead of counted as a passed check.
From an MBZ to a useful recovery signal

An operator configures a dedicated lab identity and a fingerprint tied to the actual installation. Restore jobs run in CLI workers, use Moodle locks to avoid colliding with another execution of the same archive and retain a traceable connection between the backup, temporary course and technical report.

The initial validation compares restored sections and modules against the manifest and checks selected dependency and availability information. Full file hashes, question-bank parity, completion semantics and reference integrity are not comprehensively validated, so a restored course with those unresolved checks must not be represented as fully passed.

Temporary courses are normally preserved for manual inspection. Cleanup is an explicit guarded operation and report retention is distinct from the lifetime of uploaded backup archives, which may still contain original personal data.

Install only in a protected lab: naming a site staging or setting a software flag does not block emails, webhooks or access to production resources. Database, storage and egress isolation are infrastructure responsibilities.

name: Institutional Course Blueprints
description: Create versioned institutional course templates and provision Moodle courses with native backup and restore APIs.
description_html:
Versioned course templatesNative Moodle restore

Institutional Course Blueprints

Build an institutional catalog of immutable course blueprints and provision new courses from approved revisions using Moodle's own backup and restore subsystem.

Organizations often duplicate the same course structure manually, then lose track of which model was used and which revisions changed. Course Blueprints adds reviewable template versions, dependency checks and batch provisioning without directly copying Moodle database rows.

Blueprint lifecycle
  • Create a draft blueprint from an existing course or an empty configuration.
  • Capture structural manifests and private Moodle backup artifacts.
  • Review dependencies and personal-data risks before publishing a revision.
  • Provision individual courses or batches and inspect processing history.
Immutable revisions
Publishing freezes a template revision and its archive checksums. Later changes become new revisions instead of silently rewriting an approved institutional standard.
Native provisioning
Ad-hoc workers create courses and use Moodle backup_controller and restore_controller for content that their installed components support.
Auditable operations
Each course receives a link to its source blueprint version. Request keys, locks and per-course states limit duplicate provisioning and support investigation of failures.
Standardization without hidden synchronization

Course managers create drafts, inspect the source structure and perform explicit privacy and dependency review. Approved revisions become selectable in the provisioning interface, where staff choose a target category, metadata and optional batch rows before confirming execution.

The plugin records a portable structural baseline covering sections and selected activity properties. That report is useful for detecting drift, but it does not promise complete export or comparison of grades, competencies, every question-bank detail or unsupported third-party activity data.

Courses created from a blueprint remain independent: publishing a later revision does not alter previously provisioned courses. If a restore fails after course creation, the partial course is kept for authorized review instead of being silently deleted or restored again into the same record.

Privacy review is mandatory: excluding user participation data from a Moodle backup does not guarantee that teacher-authored content, questions, attachments or plugin-specific fields contain no personal information.

name: Academic Deadline Planner
description: Analyze assignment and quiz deadline concentration across enrolled courses, with privacy-conscious scenarios for academic planning.
description_html:
Academic workloadPrivacy-aware simulations

Academic Deadline Planner

See how assignments and quizzes converge across a learner's enrolled courses, and evaluate proposed date changes without exposing individual schedules from courses outside a teacher's access.

An assignment can look perfectly reasonable in one course while five other courses also have deadlines on the same day. Academic Deadline Planner makes workload concentration visible as aggregated signals, allowing coordinators to discuss adjustments before modifying activities.

Planning tools
  • Collect assignment due dates and quiz closing dates, including supported overrides.
  • Show authorized course deadlines and export them to CSV.
  • Simulate alternative dates against aggregated enrollment-based workload.
  • Store proposals, approval decisions and a date fingerprint for review.
Cross-course context
The simulator evaluates the authorized cohort's actual enrolled courses, but does not reveal other teachers' activity names or a student-by-student timetable.
Cautious aggregation
Small-group suppression and count ranges reduce disclosure. Weighted conflict thresholds are planning heuristics, not exact workload or learning-effort measurements.
Approval before editing
Proposal review rechecks dates and permissions. Once approved, authorized staff receive a link to the native Moodle activity editor.
Simulate first, edit through Moodle

The planner refreshes course snapshots through scheduled processing and checks course-context permissions for viewers and simulations. It currently supports native assignments and quizzes; other activity types are excluded unless a reviewed provider is added.

Teachers can inspect course due dates and explore potential shifts for a selected activity. A simulation is read-only and produces aggregate workload indications rather than changing the assignment, gradebook, enrollment or quiz configuration.

Version 1.0.x intentionally does not write dates into Moodle modules automatically. The reviewer authorizes the proposal, then uses Moodle's normal activity editing interface to perform and verify the actual change. Large cohorts and unsupported extension patterns can limit the precision of the results.

Approval is not an automatic reschedule: date changes must be made in Moodle's native editor. Avoid interpreting binned workload estimates as individual learner performance data.

name: Syllabus Workflow
description: Manage course syllabus drafts, institutional templates, versioning, sequential reviews, approvals and publication in Moodle.
description_html:
Teaching plansInstitutional approvals

Syllabus Workflow

Create structured course syllabi, route them through institutional review stages and publish an approved version with preserved historical revisions and audit evidence.

A syllabus maintained as an arbitrary document or copied course description quickly loses accountability: who reviewed it, which revision was accepted and what students were shown? Syllabus Workflow turns that document into a controlled academic process inside Moodle.

Document workflow
  • Create institutional syllabus models with ordered and required sections.
  • Draft and revise teaching plans attached to individual Moodle courses.
  • Assign sequential reviewers, request changes, approve and publish.
  • Compare historical versions, inspect audit records and export printable HTML.
Structured templates
Institutional models define 19 supported content sections, such as objectives, competencies, workload, assessment criteria, schedule and bibliography.
Sequential review
Drafts progress through submitted, under-review, approved and published states. Reviewers can request changes and decisions are stored separately from immutable content snapshots.
Role-scoped publication
Teachers, reviewers, publication staff and students receive distinct permissions. Learners view published records rather than incomplete staff drafts.
Every published document has a history

Academic administrators define and version the institutional model, choose reviewer assignments and set calendar-day deadlines. Teachers fill out the plan, submit it for review and respond to requested revisions without altering an already approved snapshot.

Document versions preserve the syllabus payload and captured institutional metadata; state changes and reviewer decisions are recorded with audit information. Moodle locks and concurrency controls protect transitions when multiple authorized people work on the same plan.

Published syllabi are displayed inside the course workflow, and administrators can compare versions or export a printable HTML view. The plugin uses plain-text fields rather than accepting arbitrary HTML formatting and does not silently insert new course URL activities.

Defined scope: this edition does not provide parallel approval quorums, digitally signed documents, direct DOCX/ODT output or automatic PDF generation. Export is browser-printable HTML.

name: Super Flipbook
description: Present course PDFs as page-turning Moodle activities with page-level reading progress, completion rules and reporting.
description_html:
Interactive PDF activityReading progress

Super Flipbook

Present a PDF as a page-turning Moodle activity with page-level reading progress, optional acceptance statements and teacher reports rather than a passive downloadable file.

For training material, reading a PDF can involve requirements beyond access to the file: instructors may want to know which pages were opened, provide bookmarks and request explicit acknowledgement. Super Flipbook brings those interactions into a standard course activity.

Learner and teacher features
  • Interactive page-flip reader for a PDF uploaded to the Moodle File API.
  • Reading progress, bookmarks and private notes associated with document revisions.
  • Configurable completion criteria and optional acknowledgement text.
  • Teacher reports for viewed pages, progress, drop-off and CSV export.
Per-page activity data
Maintain page-level observations and learner progress for each PDF revision so previously recorded reading does not silently satisfy changed-document requirements.
Configurable completion
Teachers can combine unique-page coverage, estimated active time, final-page access, required pages and an explicit acknowledgement when appropriate.
Integrated course reporting
Access reports through Moodle permissions; progress can participate in course completion and gradebook workflows, subject to installation and integration verification.
A course activity, not a PDF hosting service

Documents remain in Moodle's File API and are served through its authenticated file handler. The activity uses JavaScript reader libraries to render PDF pages and provide page-turning behavior, and offers learner-facing navigation features along with instructor analytics.

The activity stores reading, page views, acknowledgements and bookmarks in separate records. Acknowledgement evidence includes the presented statement and timestamp, and optional IP recording is disabled by default. Moodle Privacy API handlers address stored learner data.

The current source is a development candidate: its PDF.js and page-flip assets must be fetched, pinned and bundled before reader testing. Real installation, gradebook, completion, backup/restore and supported-version tests remain necessary before production deployment.

Not DRM or verified attention tracking: browser-reported page time can be manipulated and authorized users can still capture PDF content. Do not describe this as cryptographic proof of reading or as a production-validated release.

name: File X-Ray
description: Inventory Moodle files through native course backup references without generating MBZ archives or deleting file contents.
description_html:
File inventoryNative backup references

File X-Ray

Inspect which Moodle file records are referenced by regular course backup operations, then compare that inventory with the files table without generating an MBZ or deleting content.

Moodle file storage often grows without a simple answer to where each file is referenced. File X-Ray builds per-course evidence from the native backup workflow and exposes file-area comparisons, while deliberately avoiding unsupported claims that every unobserved record is safe to remove.

Inventory and reporting
  • Queue a report for existing courses and process them one at a time via cron.
  • Capture backup-selected file references before the physical file-copy step.
  • Inspect per-course counts, logical bytes, progress and failed jobs.
  • Compare records by component and file area, including user and system areas.
No MBZ generation
The worker follows Moodle's backup plan up to the final file-reference collection step and stops before packaging or transferring a backup archive.
Course-by-course reports
Each run snapshots the course list, records results separately and provides paginated progress. Interrupted pending work can be resumed under locking safeguards.
Explainable file areas
The comparison groups draft, profile, private, backup, badge and H5P areas alongside discovered component file areas, with counts and logical byte totals.
Referenced is not the same as retained

The administrator generates an inventory from Site administration and allows ad-hoc tasks to process each course in sequence. The report records file references from the course backup plan and presents totals, failures and a comparison with current mdl_files records.

A file not present in this inventory may still belong to user storage, site-wide configuration, a different Moodle feature or a plugin whose backup provider does not enumerate it. It is not automatically orphaned, and the plugin neither scans filedir for physically unreferenced hashes nor offers a delete operation.

Logical file sizes and record counts are not disk-usage measurements: multiple records may point to the same contenthash. For capacity work, deduplicate hashes and verify infrastructure storage independently before deciding what can be archived or removed.

Read-only diagnostic tool: an unmatched file is an investigation lead, not deletion authorization. Partial reports and failed courses further limit the conclusions that can be drawn.
